title: SkewerJAX: Absorption Lines in Cosmological Sightlines
text: SkewerJAX: Absorption Lines in Cosmological Sightlines A pedagogical review of photon propagation, absorption processes, summary statistics, and survey analysis of cosmological skewers Review notes / working draft Abstract These notes present a compact but careful review of the main physical and mathematical ingredients involved in the generation of absorption features from gas distributed along cosmological sightlines. Their main purpose is to provide a clear and pedagogical account of the equations governing photon propagation in an expanding universe, the local formation of absorption lines, the construction of optical depth and transmitted flux, and the statistical description of the resulting flux field. Although the Ly\(\alpha\) forest analysis provides a central physical motivation, the discussion is formulated in a sufficiently general way to be useful for related absorption processes as well. A secondary motivation for these notes is to accompany SkewerJAX, a JAX-based implementation for computing absorption lines from cosmological simulations, lightcones, and related datasets. In that context, the derivations collected here are intended not only as theoretical background, but also as a practical reference connecting the underlying physics to forms that are convenient for numerical implementation. Overall, the goal is to offer a self-contained guide that can help readers build a solid understanding of the relevant equations while also serving as a useful companion for computational work. Keywords: cosmology: theory, intergalactic medium, large-scale structure of Universe, methods: numerical, quasars: absorption lines, line: profiles

title: 1 Introduction and Scope
text: These notes present a compact and pedagogical review of the main physical and mathematical ingredients needed to describe absorption features produced by gas distributed along cosmological sightlines. Their central goal is to explain, carefully and step by step, how radiation emitted by a distant source propagates through an expanding universe, interacts with intervening gas, and gives rise to observable absorption signatures in the transmitted flux. Although the Ly\(\alpha\) forest provides the main physical motivation throughout these notes, the discussion is intentionally organized in a way that is also useful for related absorption processes involving metals and high-column-density (HCD) systems. The Ly\(\alpha\) forest arises when neutral hydrogen (HI) in the diffuse intergalactic medium (IGM) imprints a dense sequence of absorption lines on the spectra of background quasars (QSOs). Because each observed wavelength can be associated with an absorption event at a different redshift along the line of sight (LoS), the forest provides a tomographic view of the high-redshift Universe. This makes it one of the most informative observables available for studying the IGM, the growth of large-scale structure (LSS), the epoch of reionization (EoR), and the connection between cosmology and baryonic physics. At large scales, Ly\(\alpha\)-forest correlations have become a precision tool for measuring cosmological distances; at smaller scales, flux statistics such as the one-dimensional flux power spectrum \(P_{\mathrm{1D}}\) carry information about the thermal and ionization history of the IGM, the shape of the matter power spectrum, neutrino mass, warm-dark-matter scenarios, and other extensions of the standard cosmological model. This is also why the subject is particularly timely. Modern spectroscopic surveys are now delivering quasar samples of unprecedented size and quality, and the statistical power of present and forthcoming analyses is increasingly limited not by the raw data volume itself, but by the quality of the theoretical modelling and by the control of systematic effects. In practice, one of the central challenges is no longer simply to detect the Ly\(\alpha\) signal, but to model it accurately enough that the information encoded in flux correlations and power spectra can be exploited without bias. Among the most important systematics in this context are contaminating absorption lines from metals and the impact of HCD absorbers, whose treatment is becoming essential for robust survey-grade analyses. A useful way to think about the problem is therefore as a forward-modelling chain: Cosmology determines the underlying dark-matter distribution. The dark-matter distribution helps shape the gas distribution and its physical state. The gas properties determine the optical depth along sightlines. The optical depth determines the transmitted flux. The transmitted flux gives rise to the survey-facing summary statistics. These notes are devoted mainly to the middle part of that chain. Our focus is on the physical and mathematical steps that connect local gas properties and atomic transition data to the observed transmitted flux, and then to the fluctuation fields and summary statistics commonly used in Ly\(\alpha\)-forest analyses. These notes are organized so that the reader can follow the full logical chain from the basic ingredients to the quantities used in current observational cosmology. We begin by introducing the minimal cosmological background required to describe photon propagation along the line of sight in an expanding universe. This provides the geometric baseline on top of which the absorption formalism is built. We then move to the local physics of absorption, deriving how the properties of the gas and of a given transition determine the line profile, the optical depth, and the transmitted flux measured by the observer. From there, we introduce normalized flux-fluctuation fields and the summary statistics constructed from ensembles of skewers or sightlines, thereby making explicit the bridge between the underlying absorption physics and the observables targeted by modern large-scale surveys. A second aim of these notes is to keep this formalism close to actual numerical practice. In contemporary Ly\(\alpha\)-forest work, one repeatedly needs to move from simulations or light-cone data products to synthetic skewers, optical depths, and statistical summaries that can be compared directly with observations. For that reason, the equations are presented in a form that preserves their physical meaning while also making clear how they can be organized for forward modelling and implementation. In particular, these notes are meant to accompany the development of SkewerJAX, a JAX-based pipeline for synthesizing absorption skewers from cosmological simulations and related datasets. Finally, it is worth stating clearly that these notes are not intended as a full review of radiative transfer, nor as a complete survey of Ly\(\alpha\)-forest phenomenology. Instead, they are designed as a structured roadmap from gas and line properties to the practical calculation of the flux. The emphasis is therefore on clarity, notation, and explicit derivation.

title: 2 Cosmological Background and Photon Trajectories
text: Before deriving the optical depth and transmitted flux, we must first specify the background spacetime in which the photons propagate. The absorption process that will be studied later does not occur in a static medium: photons travel through an expanding universe, and the gas elements that absorb them are encountered at different cosmological epochs along the line of sight. It is therefore necessary to establish how position along a photon trajectory is related to the cosmological evolution of the Universe. This section introduces that geometric background and derives the basic relation that governs the evolution of the scale factor along the ray.

title: 2.1 Minimal background cosmology
text: At the background level, we assume that spacetime is described by a Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) metric. In comoving coordinates, the FLRW line element may be written as \begin{equation} ds^2 = -\cc^2\,dt^2 + a^2(t)\left[ \frac{dx^2}{1-\kappa x^2} + x^2\,d\Omega^2 \right], \qquad \kappa \equiv -\frac{\Omega_k H_0^2}{\cc^2}. \tag{2.1} \end{equation} Here \(t\) is cosmic time, \(x\) is a radial comoving coordinate, \(d\Omega^2\) is the element of solid angle, \(H_0\) is the Hubble constant today, and \(\Omega_{k,0}\) is the present-day curvature density parameter. The expansion history is encoded in the Hubble function \begin{equation} H(a) = \frac{\dot a}{a} = H_0 \sqrt{ \Omega_{r,0} a^{-4} + \Omega_{m,0} a^{-3} + \Omega_{k,0} a^{-2} + \Omega_{\Lambda,0} }. \tag{2.2} \end{equation}

title: 2.2 Photon propagation as a null geodesic
text: Since the observables of interest are built from radiation travelling through a cosmological volume filled with gas, the natural starting point is the trajectory followed by a photon in the FLRW background. Photons propagate along null geodesics, that is, curves satisfying \(ds^2=0\). Restricting attention to radial propagation, \(d\Omega=0\), the null condition becomes: \begin{equation} 0 = -\cc^2\,dt^2 + a^2(t)\frac{dx^2}{1-\kappa x^2}, \longrightarrow \frac{dx}{dt} = \pm \frac{\cc}{a(t)}\sqrt{1-\kappa x^2}. \tag{2.3} \end{equation} This expression describes how the radial comoving position changes along the photon path. The two signs correspond simply to the orientation with which the null geodesic is parametrized. In the applications that follow, the most relevant case is that of a photon received by the observer and traced backwards into the past. In that viewpoint, one starts at the observer and moves outward along the line of sight toward progressively earlier cosmological times.

title: 2.3 Evolution of the scale factor along the line of sight
text: It is often more convenient to characterize the photon trajectory by the scale factor \(a\) as a function of comoving position \(x\), rather than by \(x(t)\) itself. In particular, our absorption formalism will require us to evaluate relative photon wavelength along the line of sight while keeping track of the cosmological epoch associated with each point. Using \(\dot a = aH(a)\), together with Eq. (2.3), the chain rule gives \begin{equation} \frac{da}{dx} = \frac{da}{dt} \frac{dt}{dx} = \pm \frac{a^2H(a)}{\cc\sqrt{1-\kappa x^2}}. \tag{2.4} \end{equation} Choose the lower (\(-\)) sign for a past-directed ray received “today” (so \(a\) decreases as \(x\) increases); choose the upper (\(+\)) sign for future-directed rays. Substituting Eq. (2.2) into Eq. (2.4), we obtain \begin{equation} \frac{da}{dx} = \pm \frac{H_0}{\cc} \sqrt{ \frac{ \Omega_r + \Omega_m a + \Omega_k a^2 + \Omega_\Lambda a^4 }{ 1-\kappa x^2 } }. \tag{2.5} \end{equation} This is the form that will be most useful later on: once a photon path is parametrized by the comoving coordinate \(x\), Eq. (2.5) specifies which scale factor, and therefore which redshift, corresponds to each point along the line of sight. Figure 1: Scale factor \(a(x)\) as a function of comoving distance \(x\) along the photon trajectory for several limiting cosmologies and for a realistic Planck-2018 background. The upper panel compares the numerical solutions of Eq. 2.5 (solid lines) with the corresponding analytical expressions when available (dashed lines) for radiation-dominated, matter-dominated, and \(\Lambda\)-dominated universes, together with the full Planck-2018 solution. The point \(x=0\), \(a=1\) marks the present-day observer. Vertical dashed lines indicate the locations where the idealized single-component solutions become singular or reach their limiting domains.

title: 2.3 Evolution of the scale factor along the line of sight
text:
2.3.1 Some Analytic Solutions

In simple Limiting cases, Eq. 2.5 can be integrated analytically. These examples are useful to build intuition and to check the consistency of numerical implementations. They show explicitly how the scale factor varies along the photon trajectory when a single component dominates the expansion. For example for matter domination: \begin{align} \int_{a_0}^{a}\frac{da}{\sqrt{a}} = \frac{H_0}{c}\int_{x_0}^{x} dx \longrightarrow a(x) = \left( a_0^{1/2} + \frac{H_0}{2c}\left(x - x_0\right)\right)^2 \tag{2.6} \end{align} For radiation domination \begin{align} \int_{a_0}^{a}da = \frac{H_0}{c}\int_{x_0}^{x} dx \longrightarrow a(x) = a_0 + \frac{H_0}{c}\left(x - x_0\right) \tag{2.7} \end{align} These analytic expressions are not meant to describe the full late-time cosmology, but rather to illustrate the structure of the solution in simple regimes. In more realistic situations, several components contribute simultaneously to \(H(a)\), and the resulting equation is typically solved numerically. See Appendix A for a brief discussion regarding how to numerically solve systems of ODEs such as Equation 2.5. Figure 1 illustrates how some of these numerical solutions compare to the analytical ones.

title: 2.4 Why this matters for the absorption formalism
text: The later derivation of the optical depth will require us to combine three ingredients along the same photon trajectory: The background cosmological evolution through \(a(x)\), The local physical state of the gas at each point of the line of sight, and The relation between the spectral coordinate measured by the observer and the wavelength locally associated with the photon when it crosses a given gas element. Once the function \(a(x)\) is known, every point along the ray can be assigned a definite cosmological epoch, and the later mapping between observer-frame and absorber-frame quantities becomes well defined. We are then in a position to move from cosmological photon propagation to the local physics of spectral absorption.

title: 3 Transmitted Flux
text: The goal of this section is to derive the formula for the transmitted flux measured by an observer from the physical properties of an intervening gas distribution. The structure below follows the same order as the actual calculation: In Sec. 3.1, we define the physical quantities that characterize the absorbing gas and the atomic transition responsible for the absorption. In Sec. 3.2, we relate the spectral coordinate measured by the observer to the wavelength locally associated with the photon when it passes through each point of the gas distribution. In Sec. 3.3, we use this local wavelength to determine how close the photon is to resonance with a given transition, and from this we construct the corresponding local absorption line profile. In Sec. 3.4, we integrate the local absorption contributions along the photon trajectory to obtain the optical depth. In Sec. 3.5, we convert the optical depth into transmitted flux. Finally, in Sec. 3.6, we introduce the associated flux-fluctuation field used in statistical analyses of ensembles of skewers or sightlines. This organization helps to separate clearly the different ingredients of the problem: the physical state of the gas, the mapping between observer and absorber, the local absorption line profile, etc. For the remaining of this section, we use the index \(i\) to denote a gas species (for example, \(\mathrm{HI}\), or \(\mathrm{SiIII}\)) and the index \(j\) to denote a specific transition associated with that species (for example Ly\(\alpha\) at \(\simeq 1215.67\,\text{\AA}\), Ly\(\beta\) at \(\simeq 1025.72\,\text{\AA}\), or SiIII transition at \(\simeq 1206.50\,\text{\AA}\)). Unless noted otherwise, the absorber is treated as a static background medium, i.e. we neglect any kind of feedback that the propagating radiation might imprint upon the gas properties.

title: 3.1 Gas and Line Properties
text: The absorption produced by a given gas-species – transition pair \((i,j)\) depends on two kinds of information: The local thermodynamical/physical state of the gas that contains the absorber, and The intrinsic atomic/molecular properties of the transition line that is being excited. For clarity, we separate the relevant quantities into gas properties, transition properties. Unless stated otherwise, \(\vec{x}\) denotes comoving position.

title: 3.1 Gas and Line Properties
text:
3.1.1 Gas properties.

The index \(i\) labels the absorbing gas species or ion under consideration (for example H I, Si II, Si III, etc.). Its local physical state is described by: \(m_i\): mass of one absorbing particle of species \(i\). Units: \(\left[\mathrm{amu}\right]\). \(n_{i\,{\rm com}}(\vec{x})\): comoving number density of absorbers. More precisely, this should be interpreted as the number density of particles in the relevant absorbing state. For a resonance line, this is usually the population of the lower level of the transition. The corresponding proper number density is \begin{align} n_{i\,{\rm phys}}(\vec{x})=\frac{n_{i\,{\rm com}}(\vec{x})}{a(\vec{x})^3}. \tag{3.1} \end{align} Units: \(\left[\mathrm{cm}^{-3}\right]\). \(T_i(\vec{x})\): kinetic temperature of the gas. This sets the thermal velocity dispersion of the absorbers and therefore the thermal Doppler broadening of the line. Units: \(\left[\mathrm{K}\right]\). \(\vec{v}_i(\vec{x})\): peculiar velocity field of the gas, i.e. the velocity relative to the pure Hubble flow. Units: \(\left[\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\right]\). \(v_{i\,\parallel}(\vec{x})\): line-of-sight projection of the peculiar velocity. This quantity shifts the local resonance condition through the Doppler effect (We will introduce this concept when presenting Eq. 3.5). Units: \(\left[\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\right]\). \(b_{i\,{\rm turb}}(\vec{x})\): microturbulent velocity dispersion. This is a phenomenological description of unresolved small-scale random motions inside the absorbing gas element. Under the usual microturbulent approximation, it broadens the line in the same Gaussian way as thermal motions. Units: \(\left[\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\right]\). Figure 2: Example of gas properties extracted from a cosmological hydrodynamic simulation. The figure shows the comoving number density \(n_{i\,{\rm com}}(\vec{x})\), the temperature \(T_i(\vec{x})\) and the peculiar velocity field \(\vec{v}_i(\vec{x})\).

title: 3.1 Gas and Line Properties
text:
3.1.2 Line properties.

The index \(j\) labels a specific transition of that species. For example, if the gas species \(i\) is neutral hydrogen HI, then different choices of \(j\) could correspond to the Ly\(\alpha\) transition at \(\simeq 1215.67\,\text{\AA}\) or the Ly\(\beta\) transition at \(\simeq 1025.72\,\text{\AA}\). Likewise, if \(i\) corresponds to SiIII, one possible choice of \(j\) is the strong resonance line at \(\simeq 1206.50\,\text{\AA}\). The transition line characteristics include: \(\lambda_j\): rest-frame wavelength of the transition. Units: \(\left[\text{\AA}\right]\). \(f_j\): absorption oscillator strength of the transition. This is a dimensionless quantity that measures the intrinsic strength of the coupling between the radiation field and the line. \(A_j\): Einstein spontaneous-emission coefficient of the upper level. Its inverse gives the radiative lifetime of the excited state, and it sets the natural (radiative) contribution to the Lorentzian width. Units: \(\left[\mathrm{s}^{-1}\right]\). \(A_{j\,{\rm coll}}(\vec{x})\): effective collisional damping rate. This term accounts for pressure/collisional broadening, i.e. the extra Lorentzian broadening produced when collisions shorten the coherence time of the transition. In the diffuse IGM this contribution is often negligible, but we keep it for generality. Units: \(\left[\mathrm{s}^{-1}\right]\).

title: 3.1 Gas and Line Properties
text:
3.1.3 Derived broadening quantities.

From the quantities above we construct the local Gaussian and Lorentzian widths that enter the line profile calculation (see Eq. 3.16). First, the thermal Doppler broadening standard deviation parameter – Units: \(\left[\mathrm{GHz}\right]\) – is given by: \begin{align} \sigma_{ij}(\vec{x}) = \frac{b_i(\vec{x})}{\sqrt{2}\lambda_j}, \qquad b_i(\vec{x})= \sqrt{b_{i\,{\rm th}}^2(\vec{x}) + b_{i\,{\rm turb}}^2(\vec{x})}, \qquad b_{i\,{\rm th}}(\vec{x})=\sqrt{\frac{2k_B T_i(\vec{x})}{m_i}}. \tag{3.2} \end{align} The Lorentzian half-width at half maximum – Units: \(\left[\mathrm{GHz}\right]\) – is \begin{align} \gamma_j(\vec{x}) = \frac{A_j + A_{j\,{\rm coll}}(\vec{x})}{4\pi}. \tag{3.3} \end{align} These quantities fully specify the local thermodynamic, kinematic, and spectroscopic ingredients needed to construct the absorption profile associated with the pair \((i,j)\).

title: 3.2 Mapping the Observed Wavelengths to the Local Gas Frame
text: The central question of this subsection is the following: given a photon that is eventually detected by an observer with wavelength \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\), what wavelength is locally associated with that same photon when it crosses a gas element at comoving position \(\vec{x}\)? This mapping is essential because the gas does not respond directly to the wavelength measured by the observer, but to the wavelength locally seen in its own frame. Once this local wavelength is known, one can determine how close the photon is to a resonance transition and therefore how efficiently it can be absorbed. To make this relation explicit, let us consider an observer frame, denoted by “obs”, located at \(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), with associated scale factor \(a_{\mathrm{obs}} = a(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{obs}})\). We denote by \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\) the wavelength with which a given photon is measured by the observer’s spectrograph. Before reaching the observer, however, that photon has propagated through the universe along a null geodesic, and its wavelength has evolved with position due to cosmological expansion and additional relativistic effects. Our goal in this subsection is therefore to express the wavelength locally associated with the photon at each point \(\vec{x}\) along its trajectory in terms of the observed wavelength \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\).

title: 3.2 Mapping the Observed Wavelengths to the Local Gas Frame
text:
3.2.1 Cosmological Redshift

We begin by accounting only for the effect of cosmic expansion. Consider a photon that is eventually detected by the observer with wavelength \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\). At an earlier point \(\vec{x}\) along its trajectory, the wavelength locally associated with that same photon is \begin{align} \lambda'\left(\vec{x}\right) = \lambda_\mathrm{obs}\,\frac{a\left(\vec{x}\right)}{a_\mathrm{obs}}. \tag{3.4} \end{align} This simply makes explicit the fact that the wavelengths of detected photons at “obs” are redshifted with respect to their wavelength in the past: the further the \(\vec{x}\) position along their trajectory we look at, the more blueshifted these photons would be.

title: 3.2 Mapping the Observed Wavelengths to the Local Gas Frame
text:
3.2.2 Doppler Effect

The previous expression accounts only for the background expansion. If the gas element at \(\vec{x}\) also has a peculiar line-of-sight velocity \(v_{i\,\parallel}(\vec{x})\), then the wavelength relevant for the interaction with that gas must include an additional Doppler shift. The corresponding local wavelength is 1: \begin{align} \lambda'\left(\vec{x}\right) = \lambda_\mathrm{obs}\,\frac{a\left(\vec{x}\right)}{a_\mathrm{obs}} \Dop^{-1}(\vec{x}), \qquad \Dop(\vec{x}) \coloneqq \sqrt{\frac{1-\beta\left(\vec{x}\right)}{1+\beta\left(\vec{x}\right)}}, \qquad \beta\left(\vec{x}\right) \coloneqq \frac{v_{i\,\parallel}\left(\vec{x}\right)}{\cc}. \tag{3.5} \end{align} Therefore, the local wavelength is obtained by combining the cosmological scaling with the Doppler correction induced by the peculiar motion of the gas. This expression could be further modified by including additional relativistic corrections, such as gravitational potential effects. However, in this work, we will consider any further contributions negligible.

title: 3.2 Mapping the Observed Wavelengths to the Local Gas Frame
text:
3.2.3 Velocity Units

The quantity introduced in this subsection is not a new physical velocity of the gas. Rather, it is a convenient reparametrization of the observed spectral coordinate (for more details check appendix B). Its main advantage is that, when the spectrum is expressed in logarithmic wavelength units, redshift acts as an additive shift (rather than multiplicative), and the separation between different transition lines becomes independent of the redshift at which the absorption occurs (see B.1). Although the observer naturally measures photons in wavelength or frequency units, it is often useful to introduce the following logarithmic coordinate, commonly referred to as velocity units: \begin{align} v_\dagger \;=\; c\ln\!\left( \frac{\lambda'(\vec{x})}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_\dagger}{a(\vec{x})} \right) = c\ln\!\left( \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{obs}}} \right), \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}} = \lambda_\dagger\, \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_\dagger}\, \exp\!\left(\frac{v_\dagger}{c}\right), \tag{3.6} \end{align} where \(\lambda_\dagger\) is a chosen anchor wavelength and \(a_\dagger\) is a reference scale factor. Therefore, \(v_\dagger\) should be understood simply as a relabelling of the observed spectral axis. Substituting this change of variable into Eq. 3.5, the wavelength locally associated with the photon at position \(\vec{x}\) becomes \begin{align} \lambda'\left(\vec{x}\right) = \lambda_\dagger\, \exp\!\left(\frac{v_\dagger}{c}\right)\, \frac{a\left(\vec{x}\right)}{a_\dagger}\, \Dop^{-1}\left(\vec{x}\right). \tag{3.7} \end{align} As previously mentioned, the usefulness of velocity units comes from the fact that, employing this logarithmic coordinate change, the separation between two different emission/absorption lines becomes redshift independent (proof on B.1). Additionally, by introducing a separate anchor wavelength normalization for different lines, \((i,j)\), corresponding to their rest-frame absorption, and setting the anchor redshift \(a_\dagger = a_f\), it is possible to re-express the different absorption processes in a common relative line-centered velocity range (see B.2): \begin{align} \lambda'_j\left(\vec{x}\right) = \lambda_j\, \exp\!\left(\frac{v_\dagger}{c}\right)\, \frac{a\left(\vec{x}\right)}{a_f}\, \Dop^{-1}\left(\vec{x}\right). \tag{3.8} \end{align} In this coordinate system all lines span the same velocity interval: for a skewer travelling from \(a(x_\mathrm{em}) = a_\mathrm{em}\) to \(a(x_{f}) = a_f\), the absorptions (neglecting peculiar velocities) would appear in the range: \begin{align} v_\dagger \in \left[ 0, \; c\ln\left(\frac{a_f}{a_{\mathrm{em}}}\right) \right]. \tag{3.9} \end{align}

title: 3.2 Mapping the Observed Wavelengths to the Local Gas Frame
text:
3.2.4 Approximated Velocity Units

There is another closely related choice of spectral coordinate often employed in practical Ly\(\alpha\)-forest calculations, and it is essentially the one implemented in packages such as fake_spectra. In this case one does not keep the exact logarithmic mapping between the observed wavelength and the local gas frame across the full light cone. Instead, one fixes a single simulation snapshot at redshift \(z_{\mathrm{box}}\), assumes that the factor \(H(z)/(1+z)\) varies only mildly across the box, and tabulates the spectrum directly on a uniform velocity grid. If \(L_{\mathrm{box}}\) denotes the comoving box size along the line of sight and \(N_{\mathrm{bins}}\) the number of spectral pixels, one may write \begin{align} u_n = n\,\Delta u, \qquad \Delta u = \frac{u_{\max}}{N_{\mathrm{bins}}}, \qquad u_{\max}\approx L_{\mathrm{box}}\, \frac{H(z_{\mathrm{box}})}{1+z_{\mathrm{box}}}. \tag{3.10} \end{align} Thus, the observed spectrum is labelled directly by a velocity-like coordinate \(u\), rather than by \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\) itself. Within this approximation, a gas element located at line-of-sight position \(x_{\parallel}\) is first assigned a Hubble-flow coordinate \begin{align} u_H(x_{\parallel}) \approx \frac{H(z_{\mathrm{box}})}{1+z_{\mathrm{box}}}\, (x_{\parallel}-x_\dagger), \tag{3.11} \end{align} and is then shifted to a redshift-space position by its peculiar velocity: \begin{align} u_{\mathrm{abs}}(x_{\parallel}) = u_H(x_{\parallel}) + s_v\,v_{i\,\parallel}(x_{\parallel}), \qquad s_v=\pm 1. \tag{3.12} \end{align} Here \(s_v\) is a sign-convention parameter: its value depends only on the adopted orientation of the spectral axis and on the sign convention used for the line-of-sight peculiar velocity. In the specific convention used by fake_spectra, the absorber-centered coordinate is implemented with a plus sign. The important point is that the calculation is then carried out directly in velocity units. For a spectral pixel labelled by \(u\), the relevant detuning from resonance is \begin{align} \Delta u(x_{\parallel};u) = u-u_{\mathrm{abs}}(x_{\parallel}), \tag{3.13} \end{align} so that the local line profile is evaluated as a function of \(\Delta u\), or equivalently of the dimensionless ratio \(\Delta u/b_i\), where \(b_i\) is the local Doppler width parameter of the absorbing gas. To first order, this is equivalent to the frequency-space description, since \begin{align} \nu_j(x_{\parallel},u) \approx -\frac{\Delta u(x_{\parallel};u)}{\lambda_j}. \tag{3.14} \end{align} Therefore, the practical single-snapshot implementation may be understood as the velocity-space version of the same construction introduced above: the spectral axis is discretized directly in velocity units, the gas element is moved to redshift space by its peculiar velocity, and the line profile is evaluated from the difference between the pixel coordinate \(u\) and the absorber-centered coordinate \(u_{\mathrm{abs}}\). It is also useful to emphasize that, in this practical formulation, the same velocity grid is used for all transitions. The dependence on the specific line \(j\) enters through the rest-frame wavelength, oscillator strength, damping coefficient, and thermal/microturbulent broadening parameters, but not through a separate choice of spectral axis for each transition. A more explicit derivation of these relations, and of their connection with the exact wavelength mapping introduced above, is presented in Appendix C. From this point onward, we denote by \(\Lambda\) the spectral coordinate used by the observer. Depending on the context, \(\Lambda\) may represent either the observed wavelength \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\), the exact logarithmic velocity coordinate \(v_\dagger\), or one of its local approximations introduced for practical calculations. Accordingly, \(\lambda'(\vec{x},\Lambda)\) denotes the wavelength locally associated with the photon labelled by \(\Lambda\) when that photon passes through the point \(\vec{x}\). This notation allows the subsequent expressions to be written independently of the particular spectral parametrization adopted. 1 In the non-relativistic limit, \(v_{i\,\parallel}\ll c\). Taylor expanding the inverse Doppler term around zero yields, at first order: \(\Dop^{-1}(\vec{x}) \approx 1 + \beta(\vec{x})\)

title: 3.3 Local Absorption Line Profile
text: We want to determine what is the line profile that would be observed by a reference frame (“obs”, see 3.2) associated with a gas source element located at \(\vec{x}\). We define the relative frequency with respect to a rest absorption wavelength \(\lambda_j\) as: \begin{align} \nu_j\left(\vec{x}, \Lambda\right) &= c\left(\frac{1}{\lambda'\left(\vec{x}, \Lambda\right)} - \frac{1}{\lambda_j}\right) \tag{3.15} \end{align} Then, we can compute the line profile: \begin{align} \phi_{ij}\left(\vec{x}, \Lambda\right) = V\left(\nu_j\left(\vec{x}, \Lambda\right);\sigma_{ij}\left(\vec{x}\right),\gamma_j\left(\vec{x}\right)\right). \tag{3.16} \end{align} Where \(V\) represents the Voigt function defined as (see Figure 3 for an example): \begin{align*} V(x;\sigma,\gamma) = \left( G\left(x';\; \sigma\right) * L\left(x';\; \gamma\right) \right)(x) \equiv \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} G(x';\sigma)\,L(x-x';\gamma)\,\mathrm{d}x' = \frac{\Re\!\big[\mathcal{W}(z)\big]}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}, \quad z=\frac{x+i\gamma}{\sqrt{2}\,\sigma}, \end{align*} Where \(\mathcal{W}\) is the Faddeeva function, and \(L\) and \(G\) represent the Lorentzian and Gaussian functions respectively: \begin{align*} L(x;\; \gamma) = \frac{1}{\pi}\,\frac{\gamma}{x^{2}+\gamma^{2}} ,\qquad G(x;\; \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\, \exp\!\left(-\,\frac{x^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right). \end{align*} Figure 3: Voigt profile evaluated for different values of \(\sigma\) and \(\gamma\). Figure 4: Line profiles for some specific transition lines: Lyman-\(\alpha\), Lyman-\(\beta\), and SiIII - 1206.50 Å. The line profiles are evaluated for different temperatures and fixed cosmological scale factors \(a\). The peculiar velocities are set to zero.

title: 3.4 Optical Depth Along the Line of Sight
text: The previous subsection defines the local absorption produced by the gas at a given point along the photon trajectory. We now turn this local description into a cumulative one. The optical depth is obtained by integrating the absorption encountered by the photon along its full path, and therefore measures the total attenuation produced by the intervening inhomogeneous gas distribution between emission and observation. In full generality, the photon propagates along a null geodesic \(\gamma\), which need not be a straight line in comoving space. The optical depth produced by transition \(j\) of species \(i\) is then written as a path integral along that trajectory: \begin{align} \tau_{ij}(\vec{x}_{\perp}, \Lambda) = \mathcal{C}_j \int_{\gamma} \frac{ n_{i\,\mathrm{com}}\!\left(\vec{x}\right) }{ a(\vec{x})^{3} } \; \phi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x},\Lambda\right) \; dl_{\mathrm{phys}}, \tag{3.17} \end{align} where \begin{align} \mathcal{C}_j \equiv \frac{e^{2}f_j}{4\varepsilon_{0}m_e c}. \tag{3.18} \end{align} This expression has a simple interpretation: at each point along the trajectory, the local contribution to the optical depth is given by the proper number density of absorbers, \( n_{i\,\mathrm{phys}}(\vec{x}) = n_{i\,\mathrm{com}}(\vec{x})/a(\vec{x})^{3}, \) multiplied by the local line profile and by the proper line element \(dl_{\mathrm{phys}}\). In many practical applications, however, the photon trajectories can be approximated as straight lines in comoving space. In that case, it is convenient to decompose the comoving position as \begin{align} \vec{x} = (\vec{x}_{\perp},x_{\parallel}), \tag{3.19} \end{align} where \(\vec{x}_{\perp}\) labels the transverse comoving position of the sightline and \(x_{\parallel}\) parametrizes the propagation along it. For a fixed sightline \(\vec{x}_{\perp}\), the optical depth becomes \begin{align} \tau_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) = \mathcal{C}_j \int_{x_{\parallel,\mathrm{em}}}^{x_{\parallel,\mathrm{f}}} \frac{ n_{i\,\mathrm{com}}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},x'_{\parallel}\right) }{ a\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},x'_{\parallel}\right)^{3} } \; \phi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},x'_{\parallel},\Lambda\right) \; a\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},x'_{\parallel}\right)\, dx'_{\parallel}, \tag{3.20} \end{align} where we used \begin{align} dl_{\mathrm{phys}} = a\,dx_{\parallel}. \tag{3.21} \end{align} Therefore, Eq. (3.20) should be understood as the straight-line approximation to the more general path-integral expression in Eq. (3.17). This form is particularly convenient in practice, since it makes explicit that the optical depth may vary from one sightline to another through its dependence on the transverse position \(\vec{x}_{\perp}\). Finally, if several transitions contribute to the absorption, the total optical depth is obtained by summing the individual contributions: \begin{align} \tau\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) = \sum_{\{i,j\}} \tau_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right). \tag{3.22} \end{align} Figure 5: Illustration of how the optical-depth integral in Eq. (3.20) maps the inhomogeneous gas distribution along a straight line of sight into absorption features in wavelength space. The upper panels show 2D slices of the number-density fields for HI (left) and SiIII (right) in the \(y\)-\(z\) plane, with the same horizontal sightline at \(z \simeq 150\,\mathrm{cMpc}\), running from \(a_{\mathrm{start}}=0.3104\) to \(a_{\mathrm{end}}=0.3333\). The colored line tracks the correspondence between position along the sightline and its spectral imprint. The two smaller panels below show the sampled profiles \(\log_{10} n(y)\) for both species along that sightline. The central panel shows the transmitted flux \(e^{-\tau}\) as a function of \(c\ln(\lambda/\lambda_{\dagger})\), with the absorption produced by Lyman-\(\alpha\) and SiIII 1206 plotted on the same spectral axis. The solid and dashed vertical markers indicate the spectral positions of the sightline endpoints for Lyman-\(\alpha\) and SiIII 1206, highlighting the shift caused by their different rest-frame wavelengths. The bottom panels show the individual transmissions for each transition separately. Overall, the figure illustrates how the final spectrum arises from the cumulative absorption of many local structures distributed along the full trajectory.

title: 3.5 Transmission and Flux
text: It is useful to distinguish between transmission, \(T(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda)\), and flux, \(F(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda)\). The transmission is the dimensionless attenuation factor produced by absorption alone, whereas the observed flux is obtained by multiplying that attenuation by the emitted continuum, \(F_0(\Lambda)\). This distinction is especially helpful when several transitions contribute simultaneously, since optical depths add while transmission factors multiply. In the straight-line approximation introduced in Sec. 3.4, the optical depth depends on both the spectral coordinate \(\Lambda\) and the transverse comoving position \(\vec{x}_{\perp}\) that labels the sightline. Accordingly, the transmitted flux and the transmission factor associated with transition \(j\) of species \(i\) are \begin{equation} F_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) = F_0(\Lambda)\, T_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right), \qquad T_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) \coloneqq \exp\!\left[-\tau_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)\right]. \tag{3.23} \end{equation} If several transitions contribute to the absorption, the total optical depth is the sum of the individual optical depths. Therefore, the total transmission along the sightline \(\vec{x}_{\perp}\) is \begin{align} T\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) &= \exp\!\left[-\tau\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)\right] = \exp\!\left[-\sum_{\{i,j\}}\tau_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)\right] = \prod_{\{i,j\}}T_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right). \tag{3.24} \end{align} The total transmitted flux is then \begin{align} F\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) = F_0(\Lambda)\,T\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) = F_0(\Lambda)\exp\!\left[-\tau\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)\right]. \tag{3.25} \end{align}

title: 3.8 Summary
4.1 Per-sample (realization-level) 3D two-point correlation, \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta\right)\)
text: Given one realization \(s\), consider the fractional fluctuation fields \(\delta_i^{(s)}(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda)\) and \(\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda)\) on a set of sightlines covering a transverse domain \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\) and the spectral interval \([\Lambda_a,\Lambda_b]\) of length \(L_\Lambda\). The per-sample 3D two-point (cross) correlation function correlates the two fields on two sightlines separated by the transverse lag \(\vec{r}_{\perp}\), at the spectral lag \(\Delta\), and averages over all the positions for which both points lie inside the available domain. With the window \begin{equation} W_{\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta}(\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda) \equiv \mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}\!\left(\vec{x}_\perp+\vec{r}_{\perp}\right)\, \mathbf{1}_{[\Lambda_a,\Lambda_b]}\!\left(\Lambda+\Delta\right), \tag{4.1} \end{equation} we define (without periodic wrap) \begin{equation} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta\right) \equiv \frac{ \int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}\! d^2x_\perp \int_{\Lambda_a}^{\Lambda_b}\! d\Lambda\; W_{\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta}(\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda)\, \delta_i^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)\, \delta_j^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp}+\vec{r}_{\perp},\Lambda+\Delta\right) }{ \int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}\! d^2x_\perp \int_{\Lambda_a}^{\Lambda_b}\! d\Lambda\; W_{\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta}(\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda) }, \qquad |\Delta| < L_\Lambda. \tag{4.2} \end{equation} The denominator is \(\left|\mathcal{A}_\perp(\vec{r}_{\perp})\right|\,(L_\Lambda-|\Delta|)\), with \(\left|\mathcal{A}_\perp(\vec{r}_{\perp})\right|\) the area of the part of \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\) whose shift by \(\vec{r}_{\perp}\) remains inside \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\) (the whole area \(|\mathcal{A}_\perp|\) for a transverse domain with periodic boundaries). The geometry of a pair and the window are sketched in Figs. 6 and 7. Figure 6: Geometry of the per-sample 3D 2PCF, Eq. (4.2). The transverse plane is the plane of the page and the line of sight points into it. The sightlines cover the transverse domain \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\) and the spectral interval \([\Lambda_a,\Lambda_b]\). The first point of a pair sits at \((\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda)\); the second is displaced by the transverse lag \(\vec{r}_\perp\), onto another sightline, and by the spectral lag \(\Delta\), along the line of sight. The estimator fixes \((\vec{r}_\perp,\Delta)\) and averages over the position \((\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda)\) of the first point. Figure 7: Window of Eq. (4.2). Left: both points must lie in \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\), so the first one is restricted to the overlap of \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\) with its copy shifted by \(-\vec{r}_\perp\) (shaded), of area \(|\mathcal{A}_\perp(\vec{r}_\perp)|\). Right: along the line of sight, for \(\Delta\ge0\), the first point is restricted to \([\Lambda_a,\Lambda_b-\Delta]\) (shaded), of length \(L_\Lambda-\Delta\). The product of both is the denominator of Eq. (4.2). Exchanging the two points of every pair gives, for real-valued fields,2 \begin{equation} \widehat{\xi}_{ji}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta\right) = \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(-\vec{r}_{\perp},-\Delta\right). \tag{4.3} \end{equation} This is an exact identity for every realization, but it requires flipping both components of the lag at once. Flipping them separately gives different statements: Transverse flip, \(\vec{r}_{\perp}\to-\vec{r}_{\perp}\) at fixed \(\Delta\): it is not an identity of the per-sample estimator, since \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\) and \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(-\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\) are built from different pairs of points. It holds for the ensemble 2PCF under isotropy around the line of sight (a rotation by \(\pi\) of the transverse plane), \(\xi_{ij}(-\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)=\xi_{ij}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\), and therefore for the per-sample estimator only on average. Combined with Eq. (4.3), it gives \(\xi_{ji}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)=\xi_{ij}(\vec{r}_{\perp},-\Delta)\). Line-of-sight flip, \(\Delta\to-\Delta\) at fixed \(\vec{r}_{\perp}\): it does not hold in general, not even for the ensemble, because the line of sight is a special direction. For a cross-correlation (\(i\neq j\)), the sign of \(\Delta\) distinguishes which of the two fields lies ahead (e.g. when the two lines are offset in the spectral coordinate), so \(\xi_{ij}(\vec{r}_{\perp},-\Delta)\neq\xi_{ij}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\). For an autocorrelation (\(i=j\)), the previous item gives \(\xi_{ii}(\vec{r}_{\perp},-\Delta)=\xi_{ii}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\) for the ensemble, again only under isotropy around the line of sight. 2 In the numerator of Eq. (4.2) for \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(-\vec{r}_{\perp},-\Delta)\), the integration runs over \(\vec{x}_\perp,\vec{x}_\perp-\vec{r}_{\perp}\in\mathcal{A}_\perp\) and \(\Lambda,\Lambda-\Delta\in[\Lambda_a,\Lambda_b]\), with integrand \(\delta_i^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda)\,\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp-\vec{r}_{\perp},\Lambda-\Delta)\). The change of variables \(\vec{x}_\perp\to\vec{x}_\perp+\vec{r}_{\perp}\), \(\Lambda\to\Lambda+\Delta\) (unit Jacobian) maps the domain onto \(\vec{x}_\perp,\vec{x}_\perp+\vec{r}_{\perp}\in\mathcal{A}_\perp\), \(\Lambda,\Lambda+\Delta\in[\Lambda_a,\Lambda_b]\), i.e. that of \(W_{\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta}\), and the integrand onto \(\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda)\,\delta_i^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp+\vec{r}_{\perp},\Lambda+\Delta)\), the numerator of \(\widehat{\xi}_{ji}^{(s)}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\). The denominators coincide by the same change of variables.

title: 4.2 Reduction to perpendicular distance, \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r_\perp,\Delta)\)
text: We write the transverse lag in polar components, \begin{equation} \vec{r}_{\perp}(r_\perp,\varphi) \equiv \left(r_\perp\cos\varphi,\;r_\perp\sin\varphi\right), \qquad r_\perp\equiv|\vec{r}_{\perp}|\ge0, \qquad \varphi\in[0,2\pi), \tag{4.4} \end{equation} and average over the direction \(\varphi\) (Fig. 8, left): \begin{equation} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\! \left(r_\perp,\Delta\right) \;\equiv\; \int_0^{2\pi}\! d\varphi\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\! \left(r_\perp\cos\varphi, r_\perp\sin\varphi,\Delta\right), \tag{4.5} \end{equation} Eq. (4.3), together with \(\varphi\to\varphi+\pi\) (i.e. \(\vec{r}_{\perp}\to-\vec{r}_{\perp}\)) gives, \begin{equation} \widehat{\xi}_{ji}^{(s)}\!\left(r_\perp,\Delta\right) = \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(r_\perp,-\Delta\right), \qquad \widehat{\xi}_{ii}^{(s)}\!\left(r_\perp,\Delta\right) = \widehat{\xi}_{ii}^{(s)}\!\left(r_\perp,-\Delta\right): \tag{4.6} \end{equation} the autocorrelations are even in \(\Delta\), while a cross-correlation is in general not (the sign of \(\Delta\) distinguishes which of the two lines lies ahead), and \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij,\mathrm{sym}}^{(s)}(r_\perp,\Delta) =\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r_\perp,\Delta)+\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r_\perp,-\Delta)\) is even. Note that \(r_\perp\) and \(\Delta\) are, in general, expressed in different units (transverse distance and spectral coordinate, respectively).

title: 4.3 Reduction to \(\mu\) wedges, \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r)\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)}\)
text: Figure 8: Left: reduction to \(r_\perp\), Eq. (4.5), with the line of sight into the page. The lags with fixed \(r_\perp\) form a cylinder around the line of sight; at each \(\Delta\), the angle \(\varphi\) is integrated around the ring of radius \(r_\perp\), which compresses the ring into the single point \((r_\perp,\Delta)\). Right: \(\mu\) wedge, Eq. (4.8), in the plane of comoving transverse and line-of-sight separations. At fixed \(r\), the wedge collects the directions with \(\mu=r_\parallel/r\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) (shaded), \(\mu=\pm1\) being the line of sight. The mirrored wedge \((-\mu_2,-\mu_1)\) (dotted) coincides with it for autocorrelations. To combine the transverse and spectral separations into a single 3D separation, both must be expressed in the same units. We can convert \(\Delta\) into a comoving line-of-sight separation, \(r_\parallel\equiv\Delta/\mathcal{J}\), with \(\mathcal{J}\equiv d\Lambda/dr_\parallel\) the local Jacobian of the spectral coordinate; in velocity units \(\mathcal{J}=H(z)/(1+z)\) (Sec. 3.2.4 and Appendix C), evaluated at the effective redshift of the interval. We then define \begin{equation} r\equiv\sqrt{r_\perp^2+r_\parallel^2}, \qquad \mu\equiv\frac{r_\parallel}{r}\in[-1,1], \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad r_\perp=r\sqrt{1-\mu^2}, \qquad \Delta=\mathcal{J}\,r\,\mu, \tag{4.7} \end{equation} where the sign of \(\mu\) keeps the sign of \(\Delta\), relevant for cross-correlations. The per-sample wedge estimator is the average of \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\) over the portion of the sphere of radius \(r\) with \(\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) (Fig. 8, right), with the solid-angle measure \(d\Omega=d\mu\,d\varphi\) (the angular part of \(d^3r=r^2\,dr\,d\mu\,d\varphi\)): \begin{align} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)} &\equiv \frac{1}{2\pi\,(\mu_2-\mu_1)} \int_{\mu_1}^{\mu_2}\! d\mu \int_0^{2\pi}\! d\varphi\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp}\!\left(r\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\varphi\right),\,\mathcal{J}r\mu\right) \notag\\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi\,(\mu_2-\mu_1)} \int_{\mu_1}^{\mu_2}\! d\mu\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(r\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\,\mathcal{J}r\mu\right), \tag{4.8} \end{align} where the second line uses Eq. (4.5). The wedge is defined for the radii at which all the lags involved are available, i.e. \(\mathcal{J}r|\mu|<L_\Lambda\) and \(\vec{r}_{\perp}(r\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\varphi)\) within the separations covered by \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\). In the extreme case \(\mu\in(-1,1)\) the wedge covers the whole sphere and gives the spherical average, \begin{equation} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(-1,1)} = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{-1}^{1}\! d\mu \int_0^{2\pi}\! d\varphi\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp}\!\left(r\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\varphi\right),\,\mathcal{J}r\mu\right) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int\! d\Omega\;\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}\right), \tag{4.9} \end{equation} i.e. the usual isotropic 2PCF \(\xi_{ij}(r)\) (the monopole of its Legendre expansion in \(\mu\)). Narrower wedges are needed only because the statistics are not isotropic in 3D: redshift-space distortions and line shifts make the correlation depend on \(\mu\), and the wedges retain that dependence. For autocorrelations, being even in \(\Delta\) (Eq. (4.6)), the wedges \((\mu_1,\mu_2)\) and \((-\mu_2,-\mu_1)\) coincide, and \(\mu\in(0,1)\) suffices.

title: 4.4 Reduction to the 1D 2PCF, \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\Delta)\)
text: The 1D 2PCF is obtained from \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\) by evaluating it at zero transverse separation, \(\vec{r}_\perp=\vec{0}\), and not by integrating it over \(\vec{r}_\perp\) (which would give a different function of \(\Delta\), mixing pairs of points on different sightlines). To derive it, it is important to keep in mind the role of the two transverse vectors in Eq. (4.2): \(\vec{x}_\perp\) is the position of the first point of the pair, i.e. the sightline on which it lies. The integral \(\int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}d^2x_\perp\) is the average over the positions of the pairs, and it is present in \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\) for every value of \(\vec{r}_\perp\). \(\vec{r}_\perp\) is the transverse separation between the two points of the pair, i.e. the argument of the 2PCF. To avoid confusion with the 3D object, we denote the per-sightline 1D estimator, whose first argument is a position and not a separation, by \begin{equation} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\rm 1D}\!\left(\vec{x}_\perp;\Delta\right) \equiv \frac{1}{L_\Lambda-\Delta} \int_{\Lambda_a}^{\Lambda_b-\Delta}\! d\Lambda\; \delta_i^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)\, \delta_j^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda+\Delta\right), \qquad 0\le\Delta<L_\Lambda . \tag{4.10} \end{equation} We then define \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\Delta)\equiv\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r}_{\perp}=\vec{0},\Delta)\), i.e. we keep only the pairs with zero transverse separation: both points lie on the same sightline (Fig. 9). Figure 9: The 1D 2PCF as a slice, Eq. (4.11). Left: only the pairs with both points on the same sightline enter (solid), averaged over all sightlines; the pairs across sightlines (dashed) do not. Right: in the \((r_\perp,\Delta)\) plane, with contours of a schematic \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r_\perp,\Delta)\), the 1D 2PCF is the function along the axis \(r_\perp=0\). Step by step: At \(\vec{r}_\perp=\vec{0}\) the window becomes \(W_{\vec{0},\Delta}(\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda)=\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}(\vec{x}_\perp)\, \mathbf{1}_{[\Lambda_a,\Lambda_b]}(\Lambda+\Delta)\). Inside \(\int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}d^2x_\perp\) the first factor is always one, and for \(\Delta\ge0\) the second one reduces the spectral integral to \(\Lambda\in[\Lambda_a,\Lambda_b-\Delta]\). The numerator of Eq. (4.2) becomes \(\int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}d^2x_\perp\int_{\Lambda_a}^{\Lambda_b-\Delta}d\Lambda\; \delta_i^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda)\,\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda+\Delta)\), where both fields are now evaluated on the same sightline \(\vec{x}_\perp\), and the denominator becomes \(|\mathcal{A}_\perp|\,(L_\Lambda-\Delta)\). Grouping the spectral integral with the factor \(1/(L_\Lambda-\Delta)\), one recognizes Eq. (4.10): \begin{align} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\Delta\right) \;\equiv\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp}=\vec{0},\,\Delta\right) &= \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_\perp|}\int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}\! d^2x_\perp\; \underbrace{ \frac{1}{L_\Lambda-\Delta} \int_{\Lambda_a}^{\Lambda_b-\Delta}\! d\Lambda\; \delta_i^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)\, \delta_j^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda+\Delta\right) }_{\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\rm 1D}(\vec{x}_\perp;\Delta)} \notag\\ &= \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_\perp|}\int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}\! d^2x_\perp\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\rm 1D}\!\left(\vec{x}_\perp;\Delta\right). \tag{4.11} \end{align} The 1D 2PCF is therefore the per-sightline 1D estimator averaged over all the sightlines: each sightline is first correlated with itself, and the results are then averaged. The integral over \(\vec{x}_\perp\) is this average over sightlines, not an integral over transverse separations. In terms of Eq. (4.5), where the integrand does not depend on \(\varphi\) at \(r_\perp=0\), \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r_\perp=0,\Delta)=2\pi\,\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\Delta)\).

title: 4.5 Ensemble 3D 2PCF
text: The ensemble 3D two-point (cross) correlation function of \(\delta_i\) and \(\delta_j\) is the ensemble expectation of their product at two points on two sightlines, \begin{equation} \xi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp\alpha},\Lambda_\alpha ; \vec{x}_{\perp\beta},\Lambda_\beta\right) \;\equiv\; \Big\langle \delta_i^{(s)}\left(\vec{x}_{\perp\alpha},\Lambda_\alpha\right)\, \delta_j^{(s)}\left(\vec{x}_{\perp\beta},\Lambda_\beta\right) \Big\rangle_{\rm ens} \;=\; \int_{\Omega}\! d\mathbb P(\omega)\; \delta_i\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp\alpha},\Lambda_\alpha,\omega\right)\, \delta_j\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp\beta},\Lambda_\beta,\omega\right), \tag{4.12} \end{equation} a deterministic function fixed by the probability law of the random fields. If the joint statistics are translation invariant both in the transverse plane and along the spectral coordinate,3 the correlation depends only on the separations \(\vec{r}_{\perp}\equiv\vec{x}_{\perp\beta}-\vec{x}_{\perp\alpha}\) and \(\Delta\equiv\Lambda_\beta-\Lambda_\alpha\): \begin{equation} \xi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp\alpha},\Lambda_\alpha ; \vec{x}_{\perp\beta},\Lambda_\beta\right) = \xi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta\right), \qquad \xi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta\right) \;\equiv\; \Big\langle \delta_i^{(s)}\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)\, \delta_j^{(s)}\left(\vec{x}_{\perp}+\vec{r}_{\perp},\Lambda+\Delta\right) \Big\rangle_{\rm ens}, \tag{4.13} \end{equation} The line of sight is a special direction (the spectral coordinate carries the peculiar velocities and the line shifts). 3 Along the line of sight this is only an approximation: different spectral positions \(\Lambda\) probe the absorbers at different redshifts, and the quantities that set the correlation (mean flux, bias, growth of structure, thermal state of the gas, and the conversion of \(\Delta\) into a comoving distance) evolve with redshift. Two pairs with the same separation \(\Delta\) but at different mean positions \(\bar{\Lambda}\equiv(\Lambda_\alpha+\Lambda_\beta)/2\) are therefore correlated differently, and strictly \(\xi_{ij}=\xi_{ij}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta;\bar{\Lambda})\). The translation-invariant form below holds when this evolution is negligible over the spectral interval considered, in which case \(\xi_{ij}\) is to be read as evaluated at an effective redshift of that interval; otherwise the interval should be split into redshift bins narrow enough for the approximation to hold within each.

title: 4.6 From per-sample to ensemble estimates
text: Suppose we have \(N\) realizations \(\{\delta_i^{(s)}(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda)\}_{s=1}^{N}\) of the fields on the same set of sightlines covering \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\). A natural estimator of the ensemble 3D 2PCF at transverse separation \(\vec{r}_{\perp}\) and spectral separation \(\Delta\) is then the average of the per-sample estimators: \begin{equation} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta\right) \;\equiv\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{s=1}^{N} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta\right), \tag{4.14} \end{equation} where \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\) is given by Eq. (4.2). Under the homogeneity of Eq. (4.13), every term in the window average of Eq. (4.2) has expectation \(\xi_{ij}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\), so each per-sample estimator, and hence their average, is unbiased: \(\langle\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\rangle_{\rm ens}=\xi_{ij}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\) (provided the \(\delta_i\) are built with the true mean fields; normalizing with means measured on the same sample introduces an integral-constraint bias at large separations). For independent realizations the variance of Eq. (4.14) decreases as \(1/N\), and the estimator converges to \(\xi_{ij}\) as \(N\to\infty\). In practice one usually has a single realization (\(N=1\)) and relies on ergodicity instead: the per-sample estimator approaches \(\xi_{ij}\) when the domain is large compared with the correlation length, i.e. when \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\) and \(L_\Lambda-|\Delta|\) contain many statistically independent patches, so that many effectively independent pairs contribute at the given lag. The identification therefore degrades for lags approaching the size of the domain (\(|\Delta|\to L_\Lambda\), or \(\vec{r}_{\perp}\) comparable to the extent of \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\)), where few pairs remain. Finally, if the statistics evolve with redshift, the estimator measures a pair-weighted average of \(\xi_{ij}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta;\bar{\Lambda})\) over the interval, i.e. the correlation at an effective redshift.

title: 5 \(P\)3D
text: This section is the Fourier-space counterpart of Sec. 4, and follows the same structure. We denote by \(\vec{k}_\perp\) the wavevector conjugate to the transverse position \(\vec{x}_\perp\), and by \(k_\parallel\) the wavenumber conjugate to the spectral coordinate \(\Lambda\) (in units of \([\Lambda]^{-1}\), e.g. \(\mathrm{s\,km^{-1}}\) in velocity units).

title: 5.1 Per-sample (realization-level) 3D power spectrum, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right)\)
text: Given one realization \(s\), with the fields \(\delta_i^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda)\) defined on \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\times[\Lambda_a,\Lambda_b]\) as in Sec. 4, we define their finite-domain Fourier transforms \begin{equation} \widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right) \equiv \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}} \int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}\! d^2x_\perp \int_{\Lambda_a}^{\Lambda_b}\! d\Lambda\; e^{-i\left(\vec{k}_\perp\cdot\vec{x}_\perp+k_\parallel\Lambda\right)}\, \delta_i^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right), \tag{5.1} \end{equation} and the per-sample 3D cross-power spectrum (periodogram) \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right) \equiv \frac{(2\pi)^3}{|\mathcal{A}_\perp|\,L_\Lambda}\; \widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right)\, \widetilde{\delta}_j^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right)^{*}. \tag{5.2} \end{equation} The normalization by the volume \(|\mathcal{A}_\perp|\,L_\Lambda\) makes \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\) independent of the size of the domain, with units \([x_\perp]^2\,[\Lambda]\). For real-valued fields, \(\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}(-\vec{k}_\perp,-k_\parallel)=\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}(\vec{k}_\perp,k_\parallel)^*\), and therefore \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ji}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right) = \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right)^{*} = \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(-\vec{k}_{\perp},-k_\parallel\right), \tag{5.3} \end{equation} the Fourier counterpart of Eq. (4.3): exchanging \(i\leftrightarrow j\) is a complex conjugation, and it is an exact identity for every realization when both components of \(\vec{k}\) are flipped at once. In particular, \(\widehat{P}_{ii}^{(s)}\) is real and even under \(\vec{k}\to-\vec{k}\), and \(\widehat{P}_{ij,\mathrm{sym}}^{(s)}\equiv\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}+\widehat{P}_{ji}^{(s)}=2\,\mathrm{Re}\,\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\). Flipping the components separately: Transverse flip, \(\vec{k}_\perp\to-\vec{k}_\perp\) at fixed \(k_\parallel\): not an identity of the periodogram; it holds for the ensemble under isotropy around the line of sight, \(P_{ij}(-\vec{k}_\perp,k_\parallel)=P_{ij}(\vec{k}_\perp,k_\parallel)\). Combined with Eq. (5.3), it gives \(P_{ij}(\vec{k}_\perp,-k_\parallel)=P_{ij}(\vec{k}_\perp,k_\parallel)^*=P_{ji}(\vec{k}_\perp,k_\parallel)\). Line-of-sight flip, \(k_\parallel\to-k_\parallel\) at fixed \(\vec{k}_\perp\): by the previous item, it is a complex conjugation. The asymmetry of a cross-correlation under \(\Delta\to-\Delta\) is therefore carried by the imaginary part of \(P_{ij}\), which is odd in \(k_\parallel\) (e.g. a relative offset \(\Delta_0\) between two lines, \(\xi_{ij}(\vec{r}_\perp,\Delta)\propto\xi(\vec{r}_\perp,\Delta-\Delta_0)\), becomes a phase \(P_{ij}\propto e^{+ik_\parallel\Delta_0}P\)). For autocorrelations \(P_{ii}\) is real and even in \(k_\parallel\).
