title: 5.3 Reduction to perpendicular wavenumber, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k_\perp,k_\parallel)\)
text: We write the transverse wavevector in polar components, \begin{equation} \vec{k}_{\perp}(k_\perp,\varphi_k) \equiv \left(k_\perp\cos\varphi_k,\;k_\perp\sin\varphi_k\right), \qquad k_\perp\equiv|\vec{k}_{\perp}|\ge0, \qquad \varphi_k\in[0,2\pi), \tag{5.5} \end{equation} and, as in Eq. (4.5), integrate over the direction \(\varphi_k\): \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k_\perp,k_\parallel\right) \;\equiv\; \int_0^{2\pi}\! d\varphi_k\; \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k_\perp\cos\varphi_k,k_\perp\sin\varphi_k,k_\parallel\right). \tag{5.6} \end{equation} Eq. (5.3) with \(\varphi_k\to\varphi_k+\pi\) gives \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ji}^{(s)}\!\left(k_\perp,k_\parallel\right) = \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k_\perp,k_\parallel\right)^* = \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k_\perp,-k_\parallel\right), \tag{5.7} \end{equation} so that, after the angular integration, the LOS flip is an exact complex conjugation for every realization: \(\mathrm{Re}\,\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k_\perp,k_\parallel)\) is even and \(\mathrm{Im}\,\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k_\perp,k_\parallel)\) odd in \(k_\parallel\), and the autocorrelations are real and even.

title: 5.3 Reduction to perpendicular wavenumber, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k_\perp,k_\parallel)\)
text:
Fourier link.

The angular integral of the plane wave in Eq. (5.4) is a Bessel function, \(\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi_k\,e^{i\vec{k}_\perp\cdot\vec{r}_\perp}=2\pi J_0(k_\perp r_\perp)\), which depends only on \(r_\perp\). If the window depends on \(\vec{r}_\perp\) only through \(r_\perp\) (e.g. for a periodic transverse domain), the angular integral over \(\varphi\) can then be carried onto \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\), and with Eq. (4.5) \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k_\perp,k_\parallel\right) = 2\pi\int_0^{\infty}\! dr_\perp\,r_\perp\,J_0\!\left(k_\perp r_\perp\right) \int_{-L_\Lambda}^{L_\Lambda}\! d\Delta\; \overline{W}\!\left(r_\perp,\Delta\right)\, \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(r_\perp,\Delta\right)\, e^{+ik_\parallel\Delta}: \tag{5.8} \end{equation} a Hankel transform in the transverse direction and a Fourier transform along the line of sight.

title: 5.4 Reduction to \(\mu\) wedges, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k)\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)}\)
text: As for the 2PCF, both components of the wavevector must be expressed in the same units. Since \(k_\parallel\Delta=(\mathcal{J}k_\parallel)\,r_\parallel\), the comoving line-of-sight wavenumber is \(\mathcal{J}k_\parallel\), and we define \begin{equation} k\equiv\sqrt{k_\perp^2+\mathcal{J}^2k_\parallel^2}, \qquad \mu\equiv\frac{\mathcal{J}k_\parallel}{k}\in[-1,1], \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad k_\perp=k\sqrt{1-\mu^2}, \qquad k_\parallel=\frac{k\,\mu}{\mathcal{J}}, \tag{5.9} \end{equation} with the sign of \(\mu\) keeping the sign of \(k_\parallel\). The per-sample wedge is \begin{align} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)} &\equiv \frac{1}{2\pi\,(\mu_2-\mu_1)} \int_{\mu_1}^{\mu_2}\! d\mu \int_0^{2\pi}\! d\varphi_k\; \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp}\!\left(k\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\varphi_k\right),\,\frac{k\mu}{\mathcal{J}}\right) \notag\\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi\,(\mu_2-\mu_1)} \int_{\mu_1}^{\mu_2}\! d\mu\; \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\,\frac{k\mu}{\mathcal{J}}\right), \tag{5.10} \end{align} and, for \(\mu\in(-1,1)\), the spherical average (monopole) \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(-1,1)} = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int\! d\Omega_k\;\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}\right) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{-1}^{1}\! d\mu\; \mathrm{Re}\,\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\,\frac{k\mu}{\mathcal{J}}\right), \tag{5.11} \end{equation} where the imaginary part drops because it is odd in \(\mu\) (Eq. (5.7)). For autocorrelations the wedges \((\mu_1,\mu_2)\) and \((-\mu_2,-\mu_1)\) coincide, and \(\mu\in(0,1)\) suffices.

title: 5.4 Reduction to \(\mu\) wedges, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k)\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)}\)
text:
Fourier link.

In comoving units \(d^2r_\perp\,d\Delta=\mathcal{J}\,d^3r\), so that, neglecting the window, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{k})=\mathcal{J}\int d^3r\;\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r})\,e^{+i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}}\). The angular average of the plane wave over the directions of \(\vec{k}\) is \(\frac{1}{4\pi}\int d\Omega_k\,e^{i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}}=j_0(kr)\), so the full-sphere wedges are related by \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(-1,1)} = 4\pi\mathcal{J}\int_0^\infty\! dr\,r^2\,j_0(kr)\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(-1,1)}. \tag{5.12} \end{equation} This one-to-one correspondence holds only for the full sphere. More generally, expanding in Legendre polynomials, \(\xi(\vec{r})=\sum_\ell\xi_\ell(r)\mathcal{L}_\ell(\mu)\) and \(P(\vec{k})=\sum_\ell P_\ell(k)\mathcal{L}_\ell(\mu)\), each multipole maps onto the same multipole, \(P_\ell(k)=4\pi\mathcal{J}\,i^\ell\int dr\,r^2\,j_\ell(kr)\,\xi_\ell(r)\), whereas a narrow wedge contains all multipoles: the Fourier transform of a \(\xi\) wedge is not the \(P\) wedge over the same \(\mu\) range.

title: 5.5 Reduction to the 1D power spectrum, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k_\parallel)\)
text: In configuration space the 1D 2PCF is the evaluation of the 3D one at \(\vec{r}_\perp=\vec{0}\) (Eq. (4.11)). In Fourier space the roles are exchanged: the 1D power spectrum is the integral of the 3D one over all \(\vec{k}_\perp\). As in Sec. 4, we start from the per-sightline objects, whose first argument is a position. The 1D Fourier transform and periodogram of the sightline at \(\vec{x}_\perp\) are \begin{align} \widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s),\rm 1D}\!\left(\vec{x}_\perp;k_\parallel\right) &\equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{\Lambda_a}^{\Lambda_b}\! d\Lambda\; e^{-ik_\parallel\Lambda}\, \delta_i^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right), \notag\\ \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s),\rm 1D}\!\left(\vec{x}_\perp;k_\parallel\right) &\equiv \frac{2\pi}{L_\Lambda}\, \widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s),\rm 1D}\!\left(\vec{x}_\perp;k_\parallel\right)\, \widetilde{\delta}_j^{(s),\rm 1D}\!\left(\vec{x}_\perp;k_\parallel\right)^*, \tag{5.13} \end{align} and the 1D power spectrum is their average over sightlines, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k_\parallel)\equiv|\mathcal{A}_\perp|^{-1}\int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}d^2x_\perp\, \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s),\rm 1D}(\vec{x}_\perp;k_\parallel)\). Step by step: Comparing with Eq. (5.1), the 3D transform is the 2D transverse transform of the per-sightline one: \(\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}(\vec{k}_\perp,k_\parallel)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}d^2x_\perp\, e^{-i\vec{k}_\perp\cdot\vec{x}_\perp}\,\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s),\rm 1D}(\vec{x}_\perp;k_\parallel)\). Parseval’s theorem in the transverse plane (with the fields set to zero outside \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\)) then gives \(\int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}d^2x_\perp\,\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s),\rm 1D}\,\widetilde{\delta}_j^{(s),\rm 1D\,*} =\int d^2k_\perp\,\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}(\vec{k}_\perp,k_\parallel)\,\widetilde{\delta}_j^{(s)}(\vec{k}_\perp,k_\parallel)^*\). Multiplying by \(2\pi/(|\mathcal{A}_\perp|L_\Lambda)\) and using Eq. (5.2), \(\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}\widetilde{\delta}_j^{(s)*}=|\mathcal{A}_\perp|L_\Lambda\,\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}/(2\pi)^3\): \begin{align} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k_\parallel\right) \equiv \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_\perp|}\int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}\! d^2x_\perp\; \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s),\rm 1D}\!\left(\vec{x}_\perp;k_\parallel\right) &= \int\!\frac{d^2k_\perp}{(2\pi)^2}\; \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right) \notag\\ &= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^2}\int_0^\infty\! dk_\perp\,k_\perp\; \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k_\perp,k_\parallel\right), \tag{5.14} \end{align} exact for every realization, the last form with Eq. (5.6). The 1D power spectrum therefore receives contributions from all transverse modes, and is a projection of the 3D one, even though the 1D 2PCF is a slice. Eq. (5.3) carries over unchanged, \(\widehat{P}_{ji}^{(s)}(k_\parallel)=\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k_\parallel)^*=\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(-k_\parallel)\).

title: 5.5 Reduction to the 1D power spectrum, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k_\parallel)\)
text:
Fourier link.

Integrating Eq. (5.4) over \(\vec{k}_\perp\), \(\int d^2k_\perp\,e^{i\vec{k}_\perp\cdot\vec{r}_\perp}/(2\pi)^2=\delta_{\rm D}^{(2)}(\vec{r}_\perp)\) selects \(\vec{r}_\perp=\vec{0}\), where \(\overline{W}(\vec{0},\Delta)=1-|\Delta|/L_\Lambda\): \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k_\parallel\right) = \int_{-L_\Lambda}^{L_\Lambda}\! d\Delta\; \left(1-\frac{|\Delta|}{L_\Lambda}\right)\, \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\Delta\right)\, e^{+ik_\parallel\Delta}, \tag{5.15} \end{equation} with \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\Delta)\) of Eq. (4.11) and, for \(\Delta<0\), \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\Delta)=\widehat{\xi}_{ji}^{(s)}(-\Delta)\) (Eq. (4.3)). The same result follows by averaging over sightlines the exact per-sightline relation between \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s),\rm 1D}\) and \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\rm 1D}\). The two reductions thus close a commuting diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{ccc} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}_\perp,\Delta\right) & \xrightarrow{\ \text{Eq.~(5.4)}\ } & \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_\perp,k_\parallel\right) \\[4pt] \Big\downarrow\;\vec{r}_\perp=\vec{0} & & \Big\downarrow\;\int d^2k_\perp/(2\pi)^2 \\[4pt] \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\Delta\right) & \xrightarrow{\ \text{Eq.~(5.15)}\ } & \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k_\parallel\right) \end{array} \tag{5.16} \end{equation} Conversely, evaluating the 3D power spectrum at \(\vec{k}_\perp=\vec{0}\) corresponds to integrating the 2PCF over \(\vec{r}_\perp\), i.e. to the correlation of the transverse-averaged fields, which is not the 1D power spectrum (Fig. 11). Figure 11: The Fourier transform exchanges slices and projections. Solid: the 1D 2PCF is the slice \(\vec{r}_\perp=\vec{0}\) of the 3D 2PCF (left), and its Fourier pair, the 1D power spectrum, is the integral of the 3D power spectrum over all \(\vec{k}_\perp\) at fixed \(k_\parallel\) (right), Eqs. (5.14) and (5.15). Dashed: conversely, the integral of the 2PCF over \(\vec{r}_\perp\) is the slice \(\vec{k}_\perp=\vec{0}\). The contours sketch a 2PCF elongated along the line of sight, whose transform is elongated along \(\vec{k}_\perp\).

title: 5.6 Ensemble 3D power spectrum
text: Under the translation invariance of Eq. (4.13) (with the same caveat on redshift evolution), the ensemble 3D power spectrum is the Fourier transform of the ensemble 3D 2PCF, \begin{align} P_{ij}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right) &\equiv \int\! d^2r_\perp\int\! d\Delta\; \xi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta\right)\, e^{+i\left(\vec{k}_\perp\cdot\vec{r}_\perp+k_\parallel\Delta\right)}, \notag\\ \xi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta\right) &= \int\!\frac{d^2k_\perp}{(2\pi)^2}\int\!\frac{dk_\parallel}{2\pi}\; P_{ij}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right)\, e^{-i\left(\vec{k}_\perp\cdot\vec{r}_\perp+k_\parallel\Delta\right)}, \tag{5.17} \end{align} equivalently characterized, for an unbounded domain, by \begin{equation} \Big\langle \widetilde{\delta}_i\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right)\, \widetilde{\delta}_j\!\left(\vec{k}'_{\perp},k'_\parallel\right)^* \Big\rangle_{\rm ens} = \delta_{\rm D}^{(2)}\!\left(\vec{k}_\perp-\vec{k}'_\perp\right)\, \delta_{\rm D}\!\left(k_\parallel-k'_\parallel\right)\, P_{ij}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right): \tag{5.18} \end{equation} homogeneity makes different Fourier modes uncorrelated, in the same way as it makes \(\xi_{ij}\) depend only on the separation. The symmetries discussed after Eq. (5.3) apply, and the reductions of the previous subsections hold for the ensemble quantities with the window set to one. In particular, the ensemble 1D power spectrum and its Fourier pair are \begin{equation} P_{ij}\!\left(k_\parallel\right) = \int\!\frac{d^2k_\perp}{(2\pi)^2}\; P_{ij}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right) = \int\! d\Delta\; \xi_{ij}\!\left(\Delta\right)\,e^{+ik_\parallel\Delta}, \qquad \xi_{ij}\!\left(\Delta\right)=\xi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{r}_\perp=\vec{0},\Delta\right). \tag{5.19} \end{equation}

title: 5.7 From per-sample to ensemble estimates
text: Given \(N\) realizations, the natural estimator is the average of the periodograms, \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right) \equiv \frac{1}{N}\sum_{s=1}^{N} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp},k_\parallel\right). \tag{5.20} \end{equation} Two differences with the 2PCF case are important.

title: 5.7 From per-sample to ensemble estimates
text:
Window bias.

Each \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r}_\perp,\Delta)\) is unbiased, but the periodogram is the Fourier transform of the tapered 2PCF, Eq. (5.4), and is therefore biased. Taking the expectation and using Eq. (5.17), \begin{align} \Big\langle\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}\right)\Big\rangle_{\rm ens} &= \int\!\frac{d^2q_\perp\,dq_\parallel}{(2\pi)^3}\; \mathcal{W}\!\left(\vec{k}-\vec{q}\right)\, P_{ij}\!\left(\vec{q}\right), \notag\\ \mathcal{W}\!\left(\vec{k}\right) &\equiv \int\! d^2r_\perp\,d\Delta\;\overline{W}\!\left(\vec{r}_\perp,\Delta\right)\,e^{+i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_\perp|L_\Lambda} \left|\int_{\mathcal{A}_\perp}\! d^2x_\perp\!\int_{\Lambda_a}^{\Lambda_b}\! d\Lambda\; e^{-i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{x}}\right|^2, \tag{5.21} \end{align} where \(\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}\) is shorthand for \(\vec{k}_\perp\cdot\vec{r}_\perp+k_\parallel\Delta\). The expected periodogram is the true power spectrum convolved with the window kernel \(\mathcal{W}\) (the Fejér kernel along the line of sight), which is normalized, \(\int d^3q\,\mathcal{W}(\vec{q})/(2\pi)^3=\overline{W}(\vec{0},0)=1\), and tends to \((2\pi)^3\delta_{\rm D}^{(3)}(\vec{k})\) as the domain grows. The bias is therefore a smoothing over \(\Delta k\sim2\pi/L\), negligible for modes much smaller than the domain, and absent for a periodic domain at the discrete modes. The analogue of the integral constraint is that normalizing with means measured on the same sample sets the \(\vec{k}=\vec{0}\) mode to zero.

title: 5.7 From per-sample to ensemble estimates
text:
Variance and averaging over modes.

Unlike \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\), whose variance at fixed lag decreases as the domain grows, the periodogram at a single mode does not converge: for Gaussian fields \(\mathrm{Var}[\widehat{P}_{ii}^{(s)}(\vec{k})]\simeq P_{ii}(\vec{k})^2\) whatever the size of the domain. A larger domain only provides more modes, spaced by \(2\pi/L\), which are approximately independent by Eq. (5.18). The ergodic estimate is thus obtained by averaging the periodogram over the modes in a bin, which is precisely what the reductions of this section do: the angular integral of Eq. (5.6), the wedges of Eq. (5.10), and the transverse integral of Eq. (5.14). The relative error then decreases as \(N_{\rm modes}^{-1/2}\), with \(N_{\rm modes}\simeq V_k\,|\mathcal{A}_\perp|L_\Lambda/(2\pi)^3\) modes in a bin of volume \(V_k\) in Fourier space, of which only half are independent, since \(\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}(-\vec{k})=\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}(\vec{k})^*\).

title: 6 \(P\)3D with the discrete Fourier transform
text: In practice the fields are sampled on a grid and the transforms of Sec. 5 are computed with a discrete Fourier transform (DFT). This section rewrites each step of Sec. 5 in discrete form, and points out what the discretization changes. Discrete objects carry their indices in square brackets.

title: 6.1 Configuration-space and Fourier-space grids
text: We take a square transverse domain of side \(L_\perp\) (\(|\mathcal{A}_\perp|=L_\perp^2\)) with \(N_\perp\times N_\perp\) sightlines on a regular grid, and \(N_\Lambda\) pixels along each sightline: \begin{align} &\vec{x}_{\perp}[\vec{n}]=d_\perp\,\vec{n}, \qquad \Lambda[m]=\Lambda_a+m\,d\Lambda, \qquad d_\perp\equiv\frac{L_\perp}{N_\perp}, \qquad d\Lambda\equiv\frac{L_\Lambda}{N_\Lambda}, \notag\\ &\vec{n}\in\{0,\dots,N_\perp-1\}^2, \qquad m\in\{0,\dots,N_\Lambda-1\}, \tag{6.1} \end{align} with \(\delta_i^{(s)}[\vec{n},m]\equiv\delta_i^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp[\vec{n}],\Lambda[m])\). We denote by \(V\equiv L_\perp^2L_\Lambda\) the volume, \(N\equiv N_\perp^2N_\Lambda\) the number of cells, and \(v\equiv V/N=d_\perp^2\,d\Lambda\) the cell volume. The DFT is defined only at the discrete modes \begin{equation} \vec{k}_\perp[\vec{p}]=\frac{2\pi}{L_\perp}\,\vec{p}, \qquad k_\parallel[q]=\frac{2\pi}{L_\Lambda}\,q, \qquad \vec{p}\in\left\{-\tfrac{N_\perp}{2},\dots,\tfrac{N_\perp}{2}-1\right\}^2, \quad q\in\left\{-\tfrac{N_\Lambda}{2},\dots,\tfrac{N_\Lambda}{2}-1\right\}, \tag{6.2} \end{equation} spaced by the fundamental modes \(k_{\rm f,\perp}\equiv2\pi/L_\perp\), \(k_{\rm f,\parallel}\equiv2\pi/L_\Lambda\) and bounded by the Nyquist wavenumbers \(k_{\rm Ny,\perp}\equiv\pi/d_\perp\), \(k_{\rm Ny,\parallel}\equiv\pi/d\Lambda\): the finite size of the domain discretizes Fourier space, and the finite resolution bounds it (Fig. 12). Figure 12: Fourier grid of the DFT, Eq. (6.2), in a plane \((k_{\perp,x},k_\parallel)\) for \(N=8\). The modes are spaced by the fundamental mode \(k_{\rm f}\) and bounded by the Nyquist wavenumber (dashed). Binning, Eqs. (6.9) and (6.10), averages the \(N_b\) modes in a shell (shaded, filled dots). Squares mark the self-conjugate modes, where \(\widetilde{\delta}\) is real. A real FFT along the line of sight stores only \(k_\parallel\ge0\) and the Nyquist plane; the hatched half follows by conjugation.

title: 6.2 Per-sample DFT periodogram, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]\)
text: With the unnormalized DFT \begin{equation} \widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}[\vec{p},q] \equiv \sum_{\vec{n}}\sum_{m=0}^{N_\Lambda-1} e^{-2\pi i\left(\vec{p}\cdot\vec{n}/N_\perp+q\,m/N_\Lambda\right)}\, \delta_i^{(s)}[\vec{n},m], \tag{6.3} \end{equation} the Riemann sum of Eq. (5.1) at the modes of Eq. (6.2) is \begin{equation} \widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_\perp[\vec{p}],k_\parallel[q]\right) \simeq \frac{v}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\,e^{-ik_\parallel[q]\Lambda_a}\,\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]. \tag{6.4} \end{equation} The phase cancels in the product of Eq. (5.2), which gives the DFT periodogram \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q] \equiv \frac{V}{N^2}\; \widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]\, \widetilde{\delta}_j^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]^* \;\simeq\; \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_\perp[\vec{p}],k_\parallel[q]\right). \tag{6.5} \end{equation} The difference between the two sides is the aliasing discussed in Sec. 6.7. Eq. (5.3) holds with the indices taken modulo the grid, \(\widehat{P}_{ji}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]=\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]^*=\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[-\vec{p},-q]\). The discreteness introduces self-conjugate modes, those with each component equal to \(0\) or to the Nyquist index \(-N/2\) (which is its own opposite modulo \(N\)): there \(\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}\) is real, so even a cross-power \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\) is real, and the odd (imaginary) part of a cross-correlation cannot be represented.

title: 6.3 Relation to the per-sample 2PCF: circular correlation and wrap-around
text: Expanding the product in Eq. (6.5) and grouping the pairs of cells by their lag \((\vec{l},m')\), using that \(e^{2\pi i\vec{p}\cdot\vec{n}/N_\perp}\) and \(e^{2\pi iqm/N_\Lambda}\) are periodic on the grid, gives the discrete Wiener–Khinchin theorem, exact for every realization: \begin{align} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q] &= v\sum_{\vec{l}}\sum_{m'=0}^{N_\Lambda-1} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\circlearrowleft}[\vec{l},m']\; e^{+2\pi i\left(\vec{p}\cdot\vec{l}/N_\perp+q\,m'/N_\Lambda\right)}, \notag\\ \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\circlearrowleft}[\vec{l},m'] &\equiv \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\vec{n}}\sum_{m} \delta_i^{(s)}[\vec{n},m]\, \delta_j^{(s)}[\vec{n}+\vec{l},m+m'], \tag{6.6} \end{align} with the indices of the second field taken modulo the grid. \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\circlearrowleft}\) is the circular 2PCF: every cell has a partner at every lag, at the price of wrapping around the edges (Fig. 13). Figure 13: Pairs of the circular 2PCF, Eq. (6.6), for \(N_\Lambda=8\) pixels at lag \(m'=3\). The \(N_\Lambda-m'\) unwrapped pairs (above) are at lag \(m'\); the \(m'\) pairs that wrap around the edge (below) are at lag \(m'-N_\Lambda\). Their fractions, \(1-m'/N_\Lambda\) and \(m'/N_\Lambda\), give Eq. (6.7), i.e. the triangular taper of Eq. (6.8).

title: 6.3 Relation to the per-sample 2PCF: circular correlation and wrap-around
text:
Periodic domain.

For a simulation box the fields are genuinely periodic, the wrapped pairs are physical pairs, and \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\circlearrowleft}\) is the discrete version of Eq. (4.2) with periodic boundaries. Eq. (6.6) is then the discrete counterpart of Eq. (5.4) with \(\overline{W}=1\).

title: 6.3 Relation to the per-sample 2PCF: circular correlation and wrap-around
text:
Non-periodic domain.

For non-periodic data (e.g. an observed spectrum along the line of sight), the wrapped pairs combine the two ends of the interval. Splitting the sum over \(m\) in Eq. (6.6) into the \(N_\Lambda-m'\) unwrapped pairs, at lag \(m'\), and the \(m'\) wrapped ones, at lag \(m'-N_\Lambda\), \begin{equation} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s),\circlearrowleft}[m'] = \left(1-\frac{m'}{N_\Lambda}\right)\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}[m'] + \frac{m'}{N_\Lambda}\,\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}[m'-N_\Lambda], \tag{6.7} \end{equation} where \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}[m']\) is the non-periodic estimator of Eq. (4.2) at the lag \(\Delta=m'\,d\Lambda\) (positive or negative); the transverse direction is treated in the same way. Since \(e^{2\pi iq(m'-N_\Lambda)/N_\Lambda}=e^{2\pi iqm'/N_\Lambda}\), inserting this into Eq. (6.6) gives \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q] = v\sum_{\vec{l}}\sum_{m'=-(N_\Lambda-1)}^{N_\Lambda-1} \overline{W}[\vec{l},m']\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{l},m']\; e^{+i\left(\vec{k}_\perp[\vec{p}]\cdot\vec{r}_\perp[\vec{l}]+k_\parallel[q]\,\Delta[m']\right)}, \tag{6.8} \end{equation} with \(\overline{W}[\vec{l},m']\) the discrete version of the window of Eq. (5.4) (\(1-|m'|/N_\Lambda\) along the line of sight): the DFT periodogram is exactly the Riemann sum of Eq. (5.4) at the discrete modes. The wrap-around is therefore not an additional error: it is the same triangular taper of the continuous finite-domain periodogram. Zero-padding the data to \(2N_\Lambda\) cells removes the wrapped pairs from Eq. (6.6), but Eq. (6.8) is unchanged and only evaluated on a finer grid, \(k_{\rm f,\parallel}\to k_{\rm f,\parallel}/2\): padding interpolates the periodogram, it neither removes the window nor adds independent modes.

title: 6.4 Reduction to perpendicular wavenumber bins, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[b,q]\)
text: On the grid, the angular integral of Eq. (5.6) becomes an average over the modes in an annulus \(b=[k_{\perp,b},k_{\perp,b+1})\): \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[b,q] \equiv \frac{1}{N_b}\sum_{\vec{p}\,:\,|\vec{k}_\perp[\vec{p}]|\in b} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q] \;\simeq\; \frac{1}{2\pi}\,\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\bar{k}_{\perp,b},k_\parallel[q]\right), \qquad \bar{k}_{\perp,b}\equiv\frac{1}{N_b}\sum_{\vec{p}\,:\,|\vec{k}_\perp[\vec{p}]|\in b}|\vec{k}_\perp[\vec{p}]|, \tag{6.9} \end{equation} with \(N_b\) the number of grid modes in the annulus; the factor \(2\pi\) comes from the unnormalized angular integral of Eq. (5.6). Two discreteness effects appear: at low \(k_\perp\) an annulus contains only a few modes, not evenly distributed in \(\varphi_k\), so the result should be assigned to the mean wavenumber \(\bar{k}_{\perp,b}\) of its modes rather than to the bin centre; and for \(k_\perp>k_{\rm Ny,\perp}\) the annuli are only partially covered by the square grid (the corners of the Fourier grid). The Bessel-function relation of Eq. (5.8) has no exact discrete counterpart, since the grid is not invariant under rotations.

title: 6.5 Reduction to \(\mu\) wedges, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[b]\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)}\)
text: Each grid mode has a definite modulus and direction, \(k[\vec{p},q]=\sqrt{|\vec{k}_\perp[\vec{p}]|^2+\mathcal{J}^2k_\parallel[q]^2}\) and \(\mu[\vec{p},q]=\mathcal{J}k_\parallel[q]/k[\vec{p},q]\), and the solid-angle integral of Eq. (5.10) becomes an average over the modes in the wedge: \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[b]\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)} \equiv \frac{1}{N_{b,\mu}} \sum_{\substack{(\vec{p},q)\,:\,k[\vec{p},q]\in b\\ \mu[\vec{p},q]\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)}} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]. \tag{6.10} \end{equation} The \(\vec{k}=\vec{0}\) mode, with undefined \(\mu\), is excluded. In comoving units the grid spacings are \(k_{\rm f,\perp}\) and \(\mathcal{J}k_{\rm f,\parallel}=2\pi\mathcal{J}/L_\Lambda\), equal only if \(L_\Lambda=\mathcal{J}L_\perp\) (e.g. the spectral extent of a cubic simulation box): otherwise the grid is anisotropic, and the number of modes per wedge depends on \(\mu\) even at fixed \(k\). At low \(k\) only a few discrete values of \(\mu\) are available, so the wedges are sparsely and unevenly populated. For \((\mu_1,\mu_2)=(-1,1)\) all the modes in the shell are averaged, and the imaginary parts cancel in pairs \((\vec{p},q),(-\vec{p},-q)\), as in Eq. (5.11).

title: 6.6 Reduction to the 1D power spectrum, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[q]\)
text: The per-sightline DFT and periodogram, the discrete versions of Eq. (5.13), are \begin{equation} \widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s),\rm 1D}[\vec{n};q] \equiv \sum_{m=0}^{N_\Lambda-1}e^{-2\pi iqm/N_\Lambda}\,\delta_i^{(s)}[\vec{n},m], \qquad \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s),\rm 1D}[\vec{n};q] \equiv \frac{L_\Lambda}{N_\Lambda^2}\, \widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s),\rm 1D}[\vec{n};q]\, \widetilde{\delta}_j^{(s),\rm 1D}[\vec{n};q]^*, \tag{6.11} \end{equation} and the 1D power spectrum is their average over the \(N_\perp^2\) sightlines. The steps of Sec. 5 carry over, with the discrete Parseval theorem in the transverse plane, \(\sum_{\vec{n}}f[\vec{n}]\,g[\vec{n}]^*=N_\perp^{-2}\sum_{\vec{p}}\widetilde{f}[\vec{p}]\,\widetilde{g}[\vec{p}]^*\), and with \(\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]\) the transverse DFT of \(\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s),\rm 1D}[\vec{n};q]\): \begin{align} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[q] \equiv \frac{1}{N_\perp^2}\sum_{\vec{n}}\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s),\rm 1D}[\vec{n};q] &= \frac{L_\Lambda}{N_\Lambda^2N_\perp^4}\sum_{\vec{p}}\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]\,\widetilde{\delta}_j^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]^* \notag\\ &= \frac{1}{L_\perp^2}\sum_{\vec{p}}\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q] = \sum_{\vec{p}}\frac{k_{\rm f,\perp}^2}{(2\pi)^2}\,\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]. \tag{6.12} \end{align} This is exactly the Riemann sum of Eq. (5.14), with cell \(k_{\rm f,\perp}^2\) in the transverse Fourier plane, and it holds identically for every realization: computing the 1D power spectrum sightline by sightline or summing the 3D periodogram over all \(\vec{p}\) at fixed \(q\) gives the same numbers, a useful check of an implementation. The sum runs only up to \(k_{\rm Ny,\perp}\): the transverse modes beyond it are not lost but aliased into the grid (Sec. 6.7), so that the expectation of \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[q]\) does not depend on the transverse sampling of the sightlines, as expected from a quantity defined sightline by sightline. Along the line of sight, Eqs. (6.6)–(6.8) reduce to \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[q] = d\Lambda\sum_{m'=-(N_\Lambda-1)}^{N_\Lambda-1} \left(1-\frac{|m'|}{N_\Lambda}\right) \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}[m']\; e^{+ik_\parallel[q]\,\Delta[m']}, \tag{6.13} \end{equation} the Riemann sum of Eq. (5.15), with \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}[m']\) the 1D 2PCF of Eq. (4.11) at \(\Delta=m'd\Lambda\), and \(\overline{W}=1\) instead of the triangle for periodic sightlines. With a real FFT along the line of sight only \(q\ge0\) is stored. For autocorrelations this is enough; for cross-correlations the negative \(k_\parallel\), needed for the odd part, is obtained from \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},-q]=\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[-\vec{p},q]^*\), i.e. from the stored \(q\ge0\) at the opposite transverse mode, while for the 1D power spectrum, after the sum over \(\vec{p}\), \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[-q]=\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[q]^*\).

title: 6.7 Ensemble expectation: aliasing, pixel window and discrete modes
text: For a homogeneous field on a periodic domain the DFT diagonalizes the covariance: the discrete counterpart of Eq. (5.18) is \begin{align} \Big\langle \widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]\, \widetilde{\delta}_j^{(s)}[\vec{p}',q']^* \Big\rangle_{\rm ens} &= \frac{N^2}{V}\, \delta^{\rm K}_{\vec{p}\vec{p}'}\,\delta^{\rm K}_{qq'}\; P_{ij}^{\rm alias}[\vec{p},q], \notag\\ P_{ij}^{\rm alias}[\vec{p},q] &\equiv \sum_{\vec{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^2}\sum_{c\in\mathbb{Z}} P_{ij}\!\left(\vec{k}_\perp[\vec{p}]+2k_{\rm Ny,\perp}\vec{a},\,k_\parallel[q]+2k_{\rm Ny,\parallel}c\right), \tag{6.14} \end{align} so that \(\langle\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}[\vec{p},q]\rangle_{\rm ens}=P_{ij}^{\rm alias}[\vec{p},q]\): the Dirac deltas become Kronecker deltas, and sampling the field at the grid points folds the power of all the modes beyond the Nyquist wavenumbers onto the grid modes (Poisson summation; Fig. 14). Figure 14: Aliasing, Eq. (6.14). On a grid of spacing \(d\), the modes \(k\) and \(k+2k_{\rm Ny}\) are indistinguishable: the power of the true spectrum beyond the Nyquist wavenumber (dashed, grey region) is folded onto \(|k|<k_{\rm Ny}\) through the shifted copies \(P(k\pm2k_{\rm Ny})\) (dotted), and the DFT measures their sum \(P^{\rm alias}\) (solid). The arrow shows one mode above \(k_{\rm Ny}\) folded onto \(k-2k_{\rm Ny}\). The aliasing is negligible when \(P_{ij}\) is small beyond \(k_{\rm Ny}\), i.e. when the pixels resolve the smallest structures of the field. For a non-periodic domain the Kronecker deltas are replaced by the window convolution of Eq. (5.21), evaluated at the grid modes and applied before the aliasing sum. If each pixel stores the average of the field over the cell rather than its value at a point (e.g. the flux integrated over an observed pixel), each term of the aliasing sum is multiplied by the pixel window, \(P_{ij}(\vec{k})\to P_{ij}(\vec{k})\,|W_{\rm pix}(\vec{k})|^2\), with \(W_{\rm pix}=\mathrm{sinc}(k_\parallel d\Lambda/2)\) along the line of sight (and the analogous factor for each transverse direction, if applicable).

title: 6.7 Ensemble expectation: aliasing, pixel window and discrete modes
section: Estimator, mode counting and the zero mode.
text:
Estimator, mode counting and the zero mode.

The estimator is the average over realizations and over the modes in a bin, Eqs. (6.9) and (6.10). For Gaussian fields the modes are independent except for the pairs \((\vec{p},q),(-\vec{p},-q)\), so a bin with \(N_b\) modes contains \(\simeq N_b/2\) independent ones and \begin{equation} \frac{\mathrm{Var}\big[\widehat{P}_{ii}^{(s)}[b]\big]}{P_{ii}[b]^2} \simeq \frac{2}{N_b}, \tag{6.15} \end{equation} except for the self-conjugate modes, which are their own partners and have \(\mathrm{Var}=2P^2\). With a real FFT, each stored mode with \(0<q<N_\Lambda/2\) stands for itself and its conjugate partner and must be counted twice when averaging over a bin, while the self-conjugate planes \(q=0\) and \(q=N_\Lambda/2\) (the Nyquist plane, equivalent to \(-N_\Lambda/2\) modulo the grid) are counted once. Finally, if the fluctuations are built with the mean of the same sample, \(\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}[\vec{0},0]=0\) identically, and this mode must be excluded from the bins; if each sightline is normalized by its own mean, \(\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s),\rm 1D}[\vec{n};0]=0\) for every \(\vec{n}\), and hence \(\widetilde{\delta}_i^{(s)}[\vec{p},0]=0\) for all \(\vec{p}\): the whole \(k_\parallel=0\) plane is removed.

title: A Systems of ODEs
text: Many of the equations that appear in these notes can be written naturally as a coupled system of first-order ordinary differential equations. This formulation is especially useful because it provides a unified way of treating several evolving quantities at once, for example, photon propagation, and optical-depth absorption along a sightline. A generic system of first-order ODEs can be written as \[ \vec{y}'(t,\vec{\theta}) = \begin{bmatrix} y_1'(t;\vec{\theta})\\ \vdots\\ y_N'(t;\vec{\theta}) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f_1\bigl(t; y_1(t;\vec{\theta}),\dots,y_N(t;\vec{\theta});\vec{\theta}\bigr)\\[2pt] \vdots\\ f_N\bigl(t; y_1(t;\vec{\theta}),\dots,y_N(t;\vec{\theta});\vec{\theta}\bigr) \end{bmatrix} = \vec{F}\bigl(t,\vec{y}(t;\vec{\theta});\vec{\theta}\bigr). \] with \[ \vec{y}(t=t_0,\vec{\theta}) = \begin{bmatrix} y_1(t=t_0;\vec{\theta}) = y_{1,0}\\ \vdots\\ y_N(t=t_0;\vec{\theta}) = y_{N,0} \end{bmatrix} = \vec{y}_0 \] This notation is intentionally general. The variable \(t\) plays the role of the independent variable, the vector \(\vec{y}\) collects all unknown functions to be solved for, and \(\vec{\theta}\) denotes any fixed parameters on which the system may depend. Writing the problem in this compact vector form is helpful because many physically different situations reduce to the same mathematical structure once the state vector and the right-hand side \(\vec{F}\) have been specified. This formulation is also the natural starting point for numerical integration. Once a problem has been cast as a first-order system with an initial condition \(\vec{y}_0\), it can be evolved using standard numerical methods such as Runge–Kutta schemes or other ODE solvers.

title: B Velocity Units Examples [3.2.3]
text: Figure 15: Schematic illustration of a photon emitted at \(x_{\mathrm{em}}\), crossing an intermediate point \(x_f\) associated with the reference scale factor \(a_\dagger\), and finally reaching the observer at \(x_{\mathrm{obs}}\) with scale factor \(a_{\mathrm{obs}}\). Let’s start observing the schematic situation depicted in Fig. 15: Suppose that two photons are emitted with rest-wavelength \(\lambda_\alpha\), one from \(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\), and another from \(\vec{x}_f\), and received at \(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) (with \(a_{\mathrm{obs}}\)). The detected wavelengths would be: \begin{align} \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}^\alpha\left(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\right) = \lambda_\alpha \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_{\mathrm{em}}} ; \qquad \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}^\alpha\left(\vec{x}_f\right) = \lambda_\alpha \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_f}, \tag{B.1} \end{align} respectively. Now, in velocity units, we have that the corresponding photons would appear at: \begin{align} v_\dagger^\alpha\left(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\right) = c \ln\left( \frac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_{\mathrm{em}}} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{obs}}} \right) = c \ln\left( \frac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{em}}} \right) ; \qquad v_\dagger^\alpha\left(\vec{x}_f\right) = c \ln\left( \frac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_{f}} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_\mathrm{obs}} \right) = c \ln\left( \frac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{f}} \right) . \tag{B.2} \end{align} Additionally, let’s consider the emission of yet two other photons (one from \(x_\mathrm{em}\) and another from \(x_f\)), but, in this case, let the associated rest-frame wavelength be \(\lambda_X\), hence: \begin{align} \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}^X\left(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\right) = \lambda_X \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_{\mathrm{em}}} ; \qquad \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}^X\left(\vec{x}_f\right) = \lambda_X \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_f}. \tag{B.3} \end{align} For the velocity units: \begin{align} v_\dagger^X\left(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\right) = c \ln\left( \frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{em}}} \right) ; \qquad v_\dagger^X\left(\vec{x}_f\right) = c \ln\left( \frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{f}} \right) . \tag{B.4} \end{align} Now we are ready to make two important remarks:

title: B.1 Redshift Independent Line Separation
text: The difference in wavelength between lines is redshift dependent, since, for a rest-frame: \begin{align} \Delta^{\alpha X}_\mathrm{rest} = \lambda_\alpha - \lambda_X. \tag{B.5} \end{align} However, our observer notices that the wavelength difference is given by: \begin{align} \Delta^{\alpha X}_\mathrm{obs} = \lambda^\alpha_\mathrm{obs}(\vec{x}) - \lambda^X_\mathrm{obs}(\vec{x}) = \left( \lambda_\alpha - \lambda_X \right) \frac{a_\mathrm{obs}}{a(\vec{x})} \tag{B.6} \end{align} This depends on the comoving position at which these lines were created. However, using velocity units, if we fix the value of the anchor wavelength, \(\lambda_\dagger\), and of the reference scale factor, \(a_\dagger\), the observed difference would be given by: \begin{align} \Delta v^{\alpha X}_\mathrm{obs} = v_\dagger^\alpha\left(\vec{x}\right) - v_\dagger^X\left(\vec{x}\right) = c \ln\left( \frac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_\dagger}{a(\vec{x})} \right) - c \ln\left( \frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_\dagger}{a(\vec{x})} \right) = c\ln\left(\frac{\lambda_\alpha}{\lambda_X}\right) = \Delta v^{\alpha X}_\mathrm{rest} \tag{B.7} \end{align} This, as promised, is redshift independent.

title: B.2 Relative Line-Centered Velocity Units
text: A second useful observation is that one can define, for each transition \(j\), a line-centered velocity coordinate by choosing the anchor wavelength to be the rest-frame wavelength of that line: \begin{align} v^{(j)} \;\coloneqq\; c\ln\left( \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}}{\lambda_j} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{obs}}} \right). \tag{B.8} \end{align} Here the superscript \((j)\) indicates that the spectral axis is being constructed using \(\lambda_j\) as the reference wavelength. In other words, this is not a new physical quantity, but simply a different way of labeling the observed spectral axis for the particular line \(j\). Now consider a photon associated with transition \(j\) that is emitted at \(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\). Its observed wavelength is \begin{align} \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}^{j}\left(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\right) = \lambda_j \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_{\mathrm{em}}}. \tag{B.9} \end{align} Substituting this into the definition of \(v^{(j)}\), we obtain \begin{align} v^{(j)}\left(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\right) &= c\ln\left( \frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_j} \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_{\mathrm{em}}} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{obs}}} \right) = c\ln\left( \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{em}}} \right). \tag{B.10} \end{align} Likewise, if a photon associated with the same transition \(j\) is emitted at \(\vec{x}_f\), then \begin{align} \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}^{j}\left(\vec{x}_f\right) = \lambda_j \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_f}, \tag{B.11} \end{align} and therefore \begin{align} v^{(j)}\left(\vec{x}_f\right) &= c\ln\left( \frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_j} \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_f} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{obs}}} \right) = c\ln\left( \frac{a_\dagger}{a_f} \right). \tag{B.12} \end{align} The key point is that, once the anchor is chosen as \(\lambda_j\), the dependence on the line wavelength cancels out completely. As a result, the position of a feature in this coordinate depends only on where along the line of sight it was produced, not on which transition is being considered. Therefore, all transitions defined in this way share the same common spectral interval: \begin{align} v^{(j)} \in \left[ c\ln\left(\frac{a_\dagger}{a_f}\right), \; c\ln\left(\frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{em}}}\right) \right]. \tag{B.13} \end{align} This is precisely why these coordinates are so useful: after centering each line on its own rest wavelength, all lines span the same velocity-domain range and can be compared on a common axis. A particularly convenient choice is \(a_\dagger=a_f\). In that case, the lower end of the velocity domain is mapped to zero, and the common interval further simplifies to: \begin{align} v^{(j)} \in \left[ 0, \; c\ln\left(\frac{a_f}{a_{\mathrm{em}}}\right) \right]. \tag{B.14} \end{align}

title: C Approximate Velocity Units in Single-Snapshot Calculations [3.2.3]
text: The goal of this appendix is to connect the exact logarithmic velocity coordinate introduced in the main text with the practical single-snapshot velocity coordinate commonly used in Ly\(\alpha\)-forest calculations, and in particular with the implementation adopted in fake_spectra. Conceptually, it is useful to distinguish three closely related objects: the exact observer-side logarithmic spectral coordinate, the approximate Hubble-flow mapping from comoving LoS position to velocity units within a single snapshot, the absorber-centered redshift-space coordinate that is finally used inside the line-profile kernel. In practical codes, the optical depth is computed directly on a uniform grid in the last of these coordinates.

title: C.1 From the exact logarithmic coordinate to the Hubble-flow approximation
text: In Appendix B we showed that, after centering the spectral coordinate on the rest-frame wavelength of a given transition \(j\), the exact logarithmic coordinate may be written as \begin{align} u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}(x) = c\ln\!\left( \frac{a_\dagger}{a(x)} \right), \tag{C.1} \end{align} where \(x\) denotes the comoving position along the line of sight, and \(a_\dagger\) is a chosen reference scale factor. To understand how this quantity changes along the skewer, we differentiate with respect to \(x\): \begin{align} \frac{d u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}}{dx} &= -c\,\frac{1}{a(x)}\frac{da}{dx} = -c\,\frac{d\ln a}{dx}. \tag{C.2} \end{align} Using \begin{align} a=\frac{1}{1+z}, \qquad \frac{d\ln a}{dz}=-\frac{1}{1+z}, \qquad dx=\frac{c}{H(z)}\,dz, \tag{C.3} \end{align} it follows that \begin{align} \frac{d\ln a}{dx} = \frac{d\ln a}{dz}\frac{dz}{dx} = -\frac{1}{1+z}\frac{H(z)}{c}, \tag{C.4} \end{align} and therefore \begin{align} \frac{d u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}}{dx} = \frac{H(z)}{1+z}. \tag{C.5} \end{align} Integrating from a reference point \(x_\dagger\), chosen such that \(u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}(x_\dagger)=0\), we obtain \begin{align} u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}(x) = \int_{x_\dagger}^{x} \frac{H[z(x')]}{1+z(x')}\,dx'. \tag{C.6} \end{align} This makes explicit that the exact logarithmic coordinate may be interpreted as the accumulated Hubble-flow contribution along the line of sight. If the redshift interval covered by one simulation box is sufficiently narrow, then the factor \(H(z)/(1+z)\) varies only mildly across the box and may be approximated by its value at the snapshot redshift \(z_{\mathrm{box}}\). In that case, \begin{align} u_H(x) \coloneqq u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}(x) \approx \frac{H(z_{\mathrm{box}})}{1+z_{\mathrm{box}}} \int_{x_\dagger}^{x}dx' = \frac{H(z_{\mathrm{box}})}{1+z_{\mathrm{box}}}(x-x_\dagger). \tag{C.7} \end{align} This is the Hubble-flow part of the practical single-snapshot coordinate.

title: C.2 From the exact wavelength mapping to the local detuning
text: We now relate the previous approximation to the exact wavelength mapping introduced in the main text. For a fixed transition \(j\), let us define an observer-side line-centered coordinate \(u\) by \begin{align} \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}} = \lambda_j\, \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_\dagger}\, \exp\!\left(\frac{u}{c}\right). \tag{C.8} \end{align} Then the exact wavelength locally associated with that photon at position \(x\) is \begin{align} \lambda'(x,u) = \lambda_j\, \exp\!\left(\frac{u}{c}\right)\, \frac{a(x)}{a_\dagger}\, \Dop^{-1}(x), \tag{C.9} \end{align} with \begin{align} \Dop(x) \coloneqq \sqrt{\frac{1-\beta(x)}{1+\beta(x)}}, \qquad \beta(x)\coloneqq\frac{v_\parallel(x)}{c}. \tag{C.10} \end{align} We now linearize each factor around the reference position \(x_\dagger\). First, \begin{align} \exp\!\left(\frac{u}{c}\right) = 1+\frac{u}{c} + \mathcal O\!\left(\frac{u^2}{c^2}\right). \tag{C.11} \end{align} Second, using Eq. (C.7), \begin{align} \frac{a(x)}{a_\dagger} = 1-\frac{u_H(x)}{c} + \mathcal O\!\left((x-x_\dagger)^2\right). \tag{C.12} \end{align} Finally, for non-relativistic peculiar velocities, \begin{align} \Dop^{-1}(x) = 1+s_v\,\frac{v_\parallel(x)}{c} + \mathcal O\!\left(\frac{v_\parallel^2}{c^2}\right), \tag{C.13} \end{align} where \(s_v=\pm1\) keeps track of the sign convention adopted for the line-of-sight peculiar velocity. Substituting these expansions into Eq. (C.9) and keeping only first-order terms, we obtain \begin{align} \lambda'(x,u) \approx \lambda_j \left[ 1+ \frac{u-u_H(x)+s_v\,v_\parallel(x)}{c} \right]. \tag{C.14} \end{align} This suggests defining the absorber-centered redshift-space coordinate \begin{align} u_{\mathrm{abs}}(x) \coloneqq u_H(x)-s_v\,v_\parallel(x), \tag{C.15} \end{align} so that Eq. (C.14) may be rewritten as \begin{align} \lambda'(x,u) \approx \lambda_j \left[ 1+ \frac{u-u_{\mathrm{abs}}(x)}{c} \right]. \tag{C.16} \end{align} Thus, in the practical single-snapshot approximation, the dependence on the gas position enters through the absorber redshift-space coordinate \(u_{\mathrm{abs}}(x)\), and the local detuning from resonance is controlled by the difference \(u-u_{\mathrm{abs}}(x)\). Using Eq. (C.16), the frequency offset defined in the main text becomes \begin{align} \nu_j(x,u) &= c\left( \frac{1}{\lambda'(x,u)}-\frac{1}{\lambda_j} \right) \approx -\frac{u-u_{\mathrm{abs}}(x)}{\lambda_j}. \tag{C.17} \end{align} Therefore, to first order, the frequency-space and velocity-space descriptions are equivalent: the same local detuning may be described either by \(\nu_j\) or by the velocity difference \(u-u_{\mathrm{abs}}\).

title: C.3 Relation to the implementation used in fake_spectra
text: The practical implementation used in fake_spectra adopts directly the velocity-space point of view. The spectrum is discretized on a uniform velocity grid, \begin{align} u_n=n\,\Delta u, \qquad \Delta u=\frac{u_{\max}}{N_{\mathrm{bins}}}, \tag{C.18} \end{align} with total span \begin{align} u_{\max}=L_{\mathrm{box}}\,v_{\mathrm{fac}}, \tag{C.19} \end{align} where \(L_{\mathrm{box}}\) is the box size along the line of sight and \(v_{\mathrm{fac}}\) is the conversion factor from comoving box units to physical \(\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). In continuum notation, this corresponds to the approximation \begin{align} u_H^{\mathrm{FS}}(x) \approx \frac{H(z_{\mathrm{box}})}{1+z_{\mathrm{box}}}\,x, \tag{C.20} \end{align} where the choice of origin is fixed implicitly by the box coordinate convention. Each gas element is then moved to redshift space by adding its line-of-sight peculiar velocity: \begin{align} u_{\mathrm{abs}}^{\mathrm{FS}}(x) = u_H^{\mathrm{FS}}(x) + v_{i\,\parallel}^{\mathrm{FS}}(x). \tag{C.21} \end{align} This is the specific sign convention adopted by the code. If one uses the opposite sign convention for \(v_{i\,\parallel}\), the same physical construction would instead be written with a minus sign. Thus, the apparent sign difference should be interpreted only as a matter of convention, not as a difference in the underlying physics. In this implementation, the line profile is not evaluated by first constructing an explicit frequency offset. Instead, one works directly with the velocity-space detuning \begin{align} \Delta u^{\mathrm{FS}}(x;u) = u-u_{\mathrm{abs}}^{\mathrm{FS}}(x), \tag{C.22} \end{align} and with the corresponding dimensionless quantity \begin{align} y_{ij}(x;u) = \frac{\Delta u^{\mathrm{FS}}(x;u)}{b_i(x)}, \tag{C.23} \end{align} where \(b_i(x)\) is the local Doppler width parameter. The Voigt/Faddeeva kernel may then be written schematically as \begin{align} \phi_{ij}(x,u) \propto \Re\!\left[ \mathcal W\!\left( y_{ij}(x;u)+i\,a_{ij}(x) \right) \right], \tag{C.24} \end{align} where \(a_{ij}(x)\) is the corresponding dimensionless damping parameter. Thus, the practical optical-depth calculation may be viewed schematically as \begin{align} \tau_{ij}(u) \propto \int dx\; n_i(x)\, \phi_{ij}(x,u) = \int dx\; n_i(x)\, \phi_{ij}\!\left( u-u_{\mathrm{abs}}^{\mathrm{FS}}(x) \right), \tag{C.25} \end{align} up to the appropriate normalization factors and kernel-weighting details. This makes explicit the central idea of the implementation: the spectrum is sampled on a universal velocity grid, each absorber is assigned a redshift-space position on that grid, and the line profile depends only on the difference between the pixel coordinate and the absorber-centered coordinate. Finally, note that this practical velocity grid is universal: it is not redefined separately for each transition. The dependence on the specific line \(j\) enters through the rest-frame wavelength, the oscillator strength, the damping coefficient, and the thermal/microturbulent broadening parameters, but the spectral axis itself is common to all transitions.
